Title: The Mental Health and Well-Being of Adults With Intellectual Disabilities During the COVID-19 Pandemic Across the UK: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Analysis
Abstract Note: Background: Research concerning the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the mental health and well-being of adults with intellectual disabilities has been cross-sectional and small scale. We examined the trajectory of mental health and well-being across the pandemic period across the UK and the factors which predicted different mental health trajectories. Method: Adults with intellectual disabilities participated in co-designed structured interviews. Four waves of data were collected between December 2020 and late 2022. At Wave 1, 621 adults with intellectual disabilities participated, with 355 at Wave 4. Well-being, pandemic anxiety, depression, anxiety, anger and loneliness outcomes were measured. Latent class mixed modelling was used to identify subgroups and within-group trajectories. Results: Well-being and pandemic anxiety remained relatively stable across time, but levels of anger, depression, anxiety and loneliness reduced gradually over time. Overall patterns masked trajectory subgroups, with differences in intercept and steepness of decline or increase in mental health problems. Different factors were generally influential for trajectory class membership and overall change across time for outcomes. Leaving the house for exercise or green spaces reported increasing well-being and reduced loneliness. Similarly, those working, volunteering or in education at Wave 1 were found to have increasing well-being and reduced loneliness, sadness and worry, and increasing wellbeing and reducing anger if they were working pre-pandemic. Conclusions: Social connection and engagement in purposeful activity were vital to maintaining the mental health and well-being of people with intellectual disabilities. Factors that were found to reduce mental well-being during the pandemic should be considered in planning for future major public health challenges and in promoting better mental well-being for people with intellectual disabilities in everyday life.

Title: The Psychometric Properties of Emotional Development Assessment tools in Intellectual Disabilities: A Systematic Review
Abstract Note: Background: People with intellectual disabilities can experience psychological distress and show behaviours of concern, such as self-injurious behaviour or physical aggression. One contributing factor is the degree to which their emotional needs are understood by those in their environment. This paper aims to review the psychometric properties of assessment tools measuring emotional development in individuals with intellectual disabilities. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted, which included 5 databases and followed the PRISMA guidance (registration number: CRD42024553322). Seven assessment tools were included in this review: the SAED, SED-S, Brief SED-S, SED-R, and SED-R2, SEO-Lukas and the Frankish model, and the psychometric properties were assessed in accordance with the COSMIN good measurement properties checklist. Results: Sixteen studies were included in this review. Internal consistency was assessed in six of the seven measures; validity was only assessed in the SAED and SED-S. Whilst both of these measures were considered reliable and valid, studies on the SAED had greater methodological quality, and the SED-S had a larger quantity of evidence. Conclusions: Both the SAED and the SED-S are psychometrically sound tools, based on the overall quality and sufficiency of the evidence. Further research should consider the usability, sensitivity and cross-cultural use, especially in UK populations.

Title: Dementia in Intellectual Disability: An Exploratory Investigation of Comorbidity Patterns and Diagnostic Outcomes
Abstract Note: Background: Dementia is more prevalent and tends to manifest earlier in individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID) compared to the general population. Acquiring specific knowledge about comorbidities and diagnostic findings in individuals with ID who have dementia, as opposed to those with ID without dementia, is essential. Such insights are crucial for enhancing the quality of care. Methods: The study was applied in a German outpatient clinic for people with ID and mental illnesses from February 2018 to September 2022. An exploratory comparison was conducted to identify differences in somatic and psychiatric comorbidities, laboratory results, cerebrospinal fluid results, neuroimaging, medication and challenging behaviour in people with ID with (n = 13, mean age: 54 years, 69% female) and without dementia (n = 73, mean age: 53 years, 48% female). Results: In this sample, persons with ID who have dementia are more likely to have Down syndrome and less likely to have affective disorders. They received antidementia drugs more often and atypical high-potency antipsychotics less often compared to persons with ID without dementia. All other clinical data showed no differences. Conclusions: Interestingly, no differences in somatic diseases (except Down syndrome) or laboratory and neuroimaging results could be found between people with ID with and without dementia. However, the diagnosis of dementia was associated with a reduced frequency of affective disorders and a reduced prescription of antipsychotics compared to the clinical sample without dementia. Due to the exploratory character of the study, replication in a much larger sample is necessary.

Title: Design, Implementation and Preliminary Results of a Comprehensive Intensive Program of Emotional and Behavioural Regulation for Children With Autism in a Hospital Context
Abstract Note: Background. Approximately 50%-70% of the autistic infantile- juvenile population presents comorbidities with mental health problems or behavioural alterations (Kanne et al., 2011). Severe emotional and behavioural dysregulation affects the adaptation to the family and school contexts (Hartley et al., 2008). An interdisciplinary integral intervention program for autistic children/ adolescents and acute functional worsening, high interference and torpid evolution, is being evaluated. The aim is to stabilize and recover the previous level of functional adaptation and to empower family/teachers to manage behavioural problems. Methods: Descriptive data are collected during 2018-2023. The intervention involves evidence-based practices (6 months). Specific clinical indicators are analysed (subsample): emergency department visits, ICG, ad-hoc Strategies Questionnaire, frequency and intensity of behavioural disturbances, understanding of ASD, ABC questionnaire, Family Empowerment Scale, and Parent Stress Index. A pre-post analysis was performed using t-student and Wilcoxon test to compare means and X2 for categorical variables. Results: Of the total sample (N = 89), (Xage 11.3 y.o, sd 0.42); 52% had Intellectual Disability (ID); 81% male. Significant changes in caregivers after the intervention (N = 25) are as follows: increase in the number of strategies used (X2 = 28, p = 0.001), understanding of ASD (X2 = 27; p = 0.001), perception of empowerment (z = -2.3, p = 0.02), and maternal stress reduction (X pre = 96.2, Xpost = 73.4; p = 0.045). In the child, reduction of ICG (Xpre = 4.04, Xpre = 1.92; p < 0.001), number of emergency room visits (Xpre = 1.38, X post = 0.052; p < 0.001), number of psychotropic drugs (Xpre = 2.64, Xpost = 2.27; p = 0.004), frequency (X2 = 24, p = 0.001), and intensity (X2 = 27, p < 0.001) of behavioural problems were observed. Additionally, a decrease of ABC irritability (Xpre = 26.9, Xpost = 18.06; p = 0.002), ABC stereotypies (Xpre = 8.03, Xpost = 5.8; p = 0.01), and ABC hyperactivity (Xpre = 23.8, Xpost; p = 0.001) was noted. An increase in the number of parent strategies predicted a reduction in the number of psychotropic drugs (r2 = 3.007; p = 0.033). Conclusions: The design of the program allows to respond to the profile of patients treated in a hospital resource. The collaborative approach between caregivers and professionals promotes the transfer of active ingredients to the natural context.

Title: Exploring Staff Training and Support Needs for Managing Challenging Behaviours in Special Schools
Abstract Note: Background: Children with intellectual disabilities exhibit challenging behaviours (CB) at a prevalence of 48%-60% (Simo-Pinatella et al. 2019), including physical or verbal aggression, self-injury, destruction, tantrums, shouting and oppositional behaviour. Staff in special education schools are frequently exposed to CB (Dworschak et al. 2016), which can impact their stress levels, well-being at work and risk of burn-out (Gilmour and Wehy 2020; McGill et al. 2018). Additionally, CB can influence intervention strategies and classroom management practices (Bowring et al. 2019). This underscores the need for a deeper understanding of the challenges faced by special education staff to ensure they receive adequate training and support for managing CB. This presentation examines staff professional preparation and support in managing CB, as well as their links to self-efficacy and the strategies they employ. It aims to identify gaps in professional preparation and contribute to more effective training approaches for CB management. Methods: An online survey was conducted in special education schools across six French-speaking cantons of Switzerland. Data were collected on participants' professional preparation, diplomas, years of experience, children's CB and class composition. The survey included three slightly adapted subtests from the Questionnaire about Teachers and Challenging Behaviours (Westling 2009), assessing (1) professional preparation regarding CB, (2) support received when dealing with CB and (3) strategies used for CB management, as well as the Self-Efficacy Belief in Dealing with CB scale (Hastings and Brown 2002). Results: A total of 205 participants completed the survey, comprising 49% teachers and 51% educators working in special education schools. Regarding experience, 44% had less than 5 years, 34% had between 5 and 15 years, and 22% had more than 15 years of professional experience. Participants reported an average class size of 6.02 students (SD = 2.5), with approximately 48% students (M = 2.88, SD = 2.08) per class displaying CB. Preliminary correlation analysis shows a positive link between the level of professional preparation and perceived self-efficacy in managing CB (r = 0.241, p < 0.001), as well as between years of experience and the reported support (r = 0.214, p = 0.003). Furthermore, when comparing staff roles, educators tend to report higher satisfaction with their professional preparation for managing CB compared to teachers (t(180) = 2.525, p = 0.012). A more in-depth analysis and key findings will be discussed during the presentation. Conclusions: Preliminary findings suggest that enhancing pre-service preparation for special education teachers could be beneficial in managing CB in students with ID. Additionally, tailored training programmes and structured support systems may help strengthen staff confidence and provide them with evidence-based strategies. In particular, in-service training programmes could play a crucial role in equipping staff with the necessary skills and resources. Further analysis will help clarify these relationships and guide the optimization of professional development initiatives to better support staff.

Title: Towards More Evidence-Based Practices in Support for People With an Intellectual Disability
Abstract Note: Background: Well-founded (scientific) knowledge and expertise of interventions are necessary to provide people with intellectual disabilities (ID) with the best possible support and services. In developing and evaluating evidence-based practices, it is important that experts by experience, professionals and researchers work closely together. By taking into account the preferences, needs and expectations of clients and the practical experience and knowledge of professionals, interventions will become relevant and practically useful. Combined with scientific knowledge, the best support can be provided. People with ID have an increased vulnerability to develop mental health problems (Cooper et al. 2007). The prevalence of mental health problems is higher in people with mild to severe ID than in people with profound ID (Mazza et al. 2019). Emotional and behavioural problems have a major impact on the person with ID themselves; their well-being and self-esteem are usually low (Lee et al. 2023). However, these challenging behaviours have consequences for caregivers and direct support staff as well. Direct support workers often experience high levels of work-related stress (Hastings et al. 2004; Skirrow and Hatton 2007). Challenging behaviours often occur in individuals who cannot sufficiently regulate their emotions independently (McClure et al. 2009). People with mild ID have an increased vulnerability to develop mental health problems and/or challenging behaviours as a result of emotion regulation problems. For people with mild ID, it can be helpful to use interventions that support them in the recognition, processing and regulation of overwhelming emotions. Direct support staff can also play an important role to help regulate emotions (Andrikos et al. 2024). It is important that direct support staff is able to regulate their own emotions well in stressful situations. Reducing stress among direct support workers can contribute to reducing challenging behaviours in people with ID (Singh et al. 2006, 2009). This symposium presents three participatory and practice-oriented studies that focus on the development and evaluation of interventions for people with ID and their context. In these studies, knowledge and experiences of experts by experience, care professionals and researchers are combined. The first two studies focus on interventions for people with mild ID (MID) or borderline intellectual functioning (BIF). The second presentation will be supplemented with a testimonial of an expert by experience about her participation in the study. The third study is about support for direct support staff of people with ID.

Title: Non-Violent Resistance in Educational Settings for Children With DID and Challenging Behaviour
Abstract Note: Background: During the last years, we recognize an increasing number of children with challenging behaviour in schools for children with disorder of intellectual development (DID). Studies from Bavaria proof this situation. Some pupils show bizarre, dangerous or destructive behaviour which hinders professionals to keep up supportive contact. This leads to feelings of insecurity and overburdening in settings of families, special care institutions and schools. Haim Omer, an Israelian psychologist, invented a concept to strengthen the presence of parents based on the idea of non-violent resistance. Within the last 20 years, the concept evolved and is known as 'New Authority'. Meanwhile, it is used as a reflecting and directing concept for professionals in many different educational and therapeutical settings. Connected with the opening of a clinic specialized in children with DID and psychiatric issues several years ago, the Blindeninstitut Würzburg installed intensive groups and classes to provide a place to live and learn for children with these diagnoses. In the meanwhile, the concept of non-violent resistance developed as a foundation and orientation for teachers, caregivers and therapists in daily work in this setting. Methods: Based on 10 years of experience in developing specialized settings for pupils with DID and psychiatric issues, the author (teacher and deputy headmaster) presents the core methods from the concept of non-violent resistance grounded in the ideas of Haim Omer to empower professionals. Relevant topics will be de-escalation and self-control, network and support, transparency and communication and vigilant concern. Results: This workshop is addressed to interested persons from all professional background, whether you are newcomer in this topic or experienced in non-violent resistance. The main aim is to discuss and share ideas, which support professional care-givers and teachers in different educational settings to be a reflected, self-controlled and open counterpart based on the aspects security, relationship and development as proposed in the concept of non-violent resistance. Conclusions: The non-violent resistance approach represents a systemically oriented alternative to traditional behaviour modification techniques. The insights from the workshop will be documented and first steps for the individual practical work will be derived. The transnational experience of the participants will enrich the collection of non-violent strategies.

Title: Adapted Dialectical Behavioural Therapy for Adults With MID-BIF and Self-Harming, Suicidal and Aggressive Behaviour
Abstract Note: Background: Individuals with mild intellectual disability (MID) and borderline intellectual functioning (BIF) are at heightened risk of developing emotion regulation and behavioural problems, such as self-harming (SH), suicidal (SUI) and/or aggressive (AB) behaviour (e.g., Nieuwenhuis et al. 2022). They have higher suicide attempt rates (Hartley et al. 2018), lower life quality and negative self-image (Brown and Beail 2009). Moreover, caregivers supporting them report elevated stress and turnover (Deveau and McGill 2016; Hastings 2002). The biosocial theory (BST) explains SH, SUI and AB as responses to genetic, developmental and personality vulnerabilities in combination with an invalidating social environment (Linehan 1993; Salavati and Selby 2025). The assumption is that SH, SUI and AB function as a temporary coping mechanism for negative cognitions and emotions (Gratz 2007) and act as maladaptive yet effective strategies to regulate emotions (Brown 2009; Woodley et al. 2021). Dialectical behavioural therapy (DBT) is based on the BST and has been developed as a treatment for borderline personality disorder (Linehan 1993), a condition known for severe emotion dysregulation, interpersonal problems and SH, SUI and AG. DBT intervenes by offering a multifaceted and intensive treatment programme aimed at learning more adaptive skills to deal with disturbing emotional experiences and (self)-destructive urges. Given the cognitive needs of individuals with MID-BIF (van den Boogaard et al. 2020), an adapted DBT protocol has been developed (Brown 2019), but evidence for its effectiveness is still lacking. Methods: Six participants with MID-BIF and emotion regulation problems entered the adapted DBT programme, limited to only skill training (n = 3) or combined to include individual therapy and telephone consultation (n = 3) (Brown 2019; Linehan 2019). Experience sampling methodology using an app (Ethica 2019) with daily diaries was used to collect data on mood and urges and the frequency of SH, SUI and AB over 134 days. Daily records of caregivers observing behavioural problems were collected as a secondary measure. Following guidelines for single-case effect studies, visual inspection and linear and logistic regression models are used to determine change (Kazdin 2013). The change interview (Elliott 2002) was conducted as a qualitative analysis to obtain a narrative of the participant's experiences of adapted DBT. Results: Insights from the interviews suggest reductions in SH, SUI and AB and improved emotion regulation skills as determinants of change. Investigations into quantitative measures are in progress and will be presented at the congress. Conclusions: Few efforts have been made investigating the effectiveness of adapted DBT in people with MID-BIF. As part of a Dutch multi-organizational project investigating the effectiveness of adapted DBT, we will discuss the results of our first preliminary attempt to establish more evidence for its effectiveness. Furthermore, with the aim of drawing more robust conclusions in the near future, we will share plans for ongoing research involving an improved, larger-scale design.

Title: Co-Production and PPIE in the Development of the PETAL Intervention
Abstract Note: Background: Aggressive challenging behaviour is prevalent in adults with intellectual disability and is associated with excessive use of restrictive practices and reduced quality of life. The development of interventions that can moderate this behaviour is a research priority for stakeholders. Such interventions should be developed with the input of people with lived experience, including adults with intellectual disability and carers. The aim of this talk is to summarize the development of a co-produced psychological intervention to support adults who display aggressive challenging behaviour in community settings, the PETAL therapy. It will also highlight the impact of Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) on both the development of the PETAL therapy and the wider research activities within the PETAL research programme. Methods: The PETAL therapy was designed following an extensive review of existing interventions and exploration of stakeholder perspectives. The content for the PETAL therapy was developed through seven co-production meetings. The co-production team included adults with intellectual disability, family carers, academics, and clinicians. Semi-structured qualitative interviews and focus group discussions were later conducted with PPIE members to explore the impact of their involvement. Results: The co-produced PETAL therapy is a seven-module tailored manualised psychological intervention to be delivered over a maximum of 14 weeks. The clinical and cost effectiveness of the PETAL therapy is currently being tested in a large-scale clinical trial. Qualitative interviews with PPIE members highlighted the value of giving a voice to adults with intellectual disability within intervention research. PPIE members felt that their expertise and input were valued by the research team, and they were able to meaningfully contribute to research activities. Conclusions: PPIE members had a profound impact on the development of the PETAL therapy and the wider research activities within the PETAL research programme. Future work should continue to develop PPIE processes to ensure the inclusion of people with lived experience in research.

Title: What Is Developmental Trauma and Why Are People With ID More Vulnerable to Trauma?
Abstract Note: We rely on the following definition of developmental trauma by the Complex Trauma taskforce of the National Child Traumatic Stress Network: 'Developmental trauma is the experience of multiple, chronic and prolonged, developmentally adverse traumatic events, most often of an interpersonal nature and early-life onset' (van der Kolk et al. 2005, 2). We will discuss two obstacles in the support of people with ID and developmental trauma. First, people with ID are more likely to experience this developmental trauma. This is because they experience more risk factors for trauma due to their disability and life circumstances. In addition, they often have fewer protective factors. Second, trauma is often not recognized in people with ID. Many forms of interpersonal trauma do not meet the criteria for PTSD in the classification instrument DSM-V. As a result, trauma is often not diagnosed. In addition, psychological and behavioural problems linked to trauma are often incorrectly explained from intellectual disability itself or other diagnoses (e.g., ADHD, ASD, mood disorder and anxiety disorder). By not recognizing trauma, appropriate support and treatment are not provided. Therefore, it is important to clarify traumatic experiences when we are supporting someone.

Title: Exploring Stress and Stress Regulation in People With Severe to Profound Intellectual Disabilities (SPID): A Scoping Review
Abstract Note: Background: People with severe to profound intellectual disabilities (SPID) become easily overwhelmed by stimuli. This can lead to responses like withdrawal, self-protective behaviours, or challenging behaviours such as self-injury or aggression. The limited abilities of persons with SPID to autonomously cope with stress can be understood from the profoundness and the complexity of their disabilities. Knowledge on how sensory or internal stimuli impact a person's stress level, how they try to cope with this stress themselves, how co-regulation by a person's caregiver can be effectively realized, and how stress regulation affects emotional wellbeing and engagement is necessary to improve the quality of life and learning opportunities for persons with SPID. However, current literature lacks comprehensive insights into how these individuals experience and react to stimuli in daily life and how caregivers can effectively co-regulate stress. Method: As a first step in a broader project, we conducted a scoping review to provide an overview of the literature on stress and stress regulation in people with severe to profound intellectual disabilities and to explore different strategies and interventions to manage and regulate stress of people with SPID. Review Questions: 1. What are the study characteristics of existing research on stress and stress regulation in people with SPID? 2. How is the methodological quality of the included studies, as assessed by the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT)? 3. Which methods are used to assess stress and stress regulation? 4. Which internal and external stressors are described/measured in the literature? 5. What strategies or interventions, used by the person with SPID or the environment, are described in the current literature to manage these stressors? Results: This review aimed to explore current knowledge on stress and stress regulation in people with SPID and revealed important knowledge gaps in the literature. The data extraction and analysis process are still ongoing. The main results will be presented during the presentation. Conclusions: The scoping review concludes by giving a descriptive overview of different sources of stress and interventions to manage this stress in persons with SPID. The results and conclusions of the scoping review will be presented comprehensively.

Title: Prevalence of Schizophrenia in Children, Adults and Older People With Intellectual Disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: The knowledge about the prevalence of schizophrenia among people with intellectual disabilities (ID) is sparse, particularly concerning the distribution in different age groups. Methods: This was an 8-year longitudinal register study, including all residents of Skåne (south of Sweden) on 1 January 2014. People with a diagnosis of ID or Down syndrome, or service and support for people with ID/autism spectrum disorder, constituted the ID cohort (n = 14 716). After excluding family members of people in the ID cohort, the remaining population of Skåne comprised the gPop cohort (n = 1 226 955). The primary outcome measure was having at least one diagnosis in the schizophrenia spectrum. Secondary outcomes were single diagnoses within the schizophrenia spectrum. Results: The aim was to investigate the prevalence of diagnoses in the schizophrenia spectrum among people with ID compared with the general population (gPop). The prevalence of schizophrenia spectrum diagnoses was 7.2% in the ID cohort. This was more than an eightfold increase compared with the gPop. The risk was also high among children (aged 0-18 years at the start of the study period), RR = 9.42. Those with a diagnosis of Down Syndrome, the risk of schizophrenia diagnosis was more than twice as high as in gPop. Concomitant ASD or genetic syndrome did not carry an excess risk among people with ID when compared with the gPop. Conclusions: The findings support earlier assumptions that people with vulnerable brains develop psychotic disorders more often and that the onset age is lower than among people in the gPop. Habilitation services for children and adolescents, as well as general mental health services, should keep in mind that schizophrenia may be present when children and adolescents show severely decreased functioning, anxiety or aggressive behaviour.

Title: Screening and Classification of PTSD in Adults With Mild Intellectual Disability
Abstract Note: Background: Individuals with Mild Intellectual Disability or Borderline Intellectual Functioning (MID-BIF) are at a high risk of developing post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). No screening instrument for PTSD (based on the DSM-5- TR) in people with MID-BIF exists for this group. The first study aimed to evaluate the validity of the Trauma Screener Intellectual Disability (TS-ID) in adults with MID-BIF and determine the optimal cut-off value for an optimal specificity-sensitivity ratio compared with a PTSD diagnosis. The second study assessed the reliability and construct validity of the Diagnostic Interview Trauma and Stressors- Intellectual Disability-Adult version (DITS-ID- adults) in this population. These studies aim to improve PTSD recognition and classification in individuals with MID-BIF. Methods: We adapted the Child and Adolescent Trauma Screener (KJTS) for adults with MID-BIF into the TS-ID. The TS-ID and Diagnostic Interview Trauma and Stressors- Intellectual Disability-Adult version (DITS-ID adults) were administered to 97 participants with MID-BIF in supported housing. Additionally, the Brief Symptom Inventory-18 (BSI-18) and Impact of Event Scale-Intellectual Disability (IES-ID) were administered to the 97 participants. The Anxiety, Depression, and Mood Scale (ADESS) and Behaviour Problems Inventory (BPI) were administered to their relatives. Results: The TS-ID adult version showed high internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.94) and excellent validity (AUC = 0.94) for distinguishing PTSD in adults with MID-BIF. Optimal specificity and sensitivity was found at a cutoff score of 18. Although the TS-ID proxy version demonstrated excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.93), it showed no validity in distinguishing PTSD in adults with MID-BIF. The interrater reliability of the DITS-ID- adults was good to excellent. The construct validity of the DITS-ID- adults was good, based on positive correlations between the BSI-18, IES-ID, ADESS and DITS-ID- adults and mainly positive correlations between the BPI and DITS-ID- adults (r = 0.21 to r = 0.75). Reporting potentially traumatic events listed under the A criterium for PTSD was associated with fulfilling PTSD symptom criteria. In this sample, 58% were classified with PTSD according to the DITS-ID- adults, while PTSD diagnosis on file was low (7%). Conclusions: The TS-ID demonstrated favourable psychometric qualities as a screening tool for PTSD in individuals with MID-BIF. The findings also support the DITS-ID- adults as a reliable and valid tool for classifying PTSD in this population.

Title: Focus on the Body: Psychomotor Diagnostics and Interventions for People With Intellectual Disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: Body-and movement-oriented diagnostics and interventions, such as psychomotor assessment and treatment, are widely used in Dutch clinical practice in people with mild intellectual disability or borderline intellectual functioning (MID-BIF). The aim is to address psychological and behavioural problems, such as (sexual) trauma, aggressive behaviour or interaction problems. Both psychomotor assessment and treatment emphasize body experience, recognizing its role in emotion and arousal regulation, and the ability to express needs and set boundaries in social relationships. The experiential character of psychomotor therapy matches the needs and learning style of people with MID-BIF. The approach actively evokes here-and- now experiences in a therapeutic setting and provides a save context to practice new and adequate behaviour. In this symposium, different examples of quantitative and qualitative research on this largely nonverbal approach will be presented. Findings will be shared on the assessment of body experience in adults with MID-BIF who were sexually abused, as well as on the effectiveness of psychomotor therapy in treating the consequences of sexual trauma in this group. Additionally, research on two psychomotor interventions will be discussed: one addressing aggressive behaviour in adults with MID-BIF and another focusing on interaction problems in children with MID-BIF and their parents. Although the potential of body-and movement-oriented diagnostics and treatment to enhance therapeutic outcomes is evident in clinical practice, there is still limited research on this approach in people with MID-BIF. This symposium aims to bridge the gap between clinical practice and research by highlighting current research findings and discussing its implications for the field.

Title: Atelier Tam-Tam: An Integrated Project: Mental Health Workers Meet Dual Diagnosis Patients With Positive Outcome for Both
Abstract Note: Background: Thirteen years ago, Belgium's mental health reform (Article 107), inspired by the Birmingham model, led to the closure of chronic psychiatric beds in favour of ambulatory care. For 14 years, Dr Godelieve Baetens led a dual diagnosis unit for individuals with intellectual disabilities and psychiatric disorders, often displaying severe aggression. In collaboration with psychoanalyst Monique Damave, they developed a therapeutic approach that significantly reduced behavioural crises by fostering personal and emotional differentiation through structured therapeutic workshops. Over 3 months, patients progressed from stability within the unit to better integration in the institute and, eventually, in their family or residence. With the reform limiting crisis treatment to 3 weeks, they developed an outpatient therapeutic programme, ensuring patients could continue their intimate differentiation in real-world settings. Early results have been promising, and to share our findings, they launched a training programme combining theory and practice-also with highly satisfactory outcomes. Methods: Atelier Tam-Tam applies the principles of therapeutic workshops to help individuals with dual diagnosis regulate their emotions in a structured and secure space. Through entry and exit rituals, participants transition smoothly into and out of the workshop, fostering engagement and emotional stability. A defined role framework ensures a predictable environment where individuals can safely explore new ways of interacting, supported by facilitators who guide their process. Triangulation between participants, facilitators and the group allows for emotional expression, mediation and co-regulation, reinforcing self-awareness and social adaptability. By integrating these elements, Atelier Tam-Tam serves as a 'laboratory' where participants develop coping strategies and resilience, better preparing them for external challenges. Results: Atelier Tam-Tam pursues a dual mission: • Educate and train: Our objective is to increase the number of professionals who are aware of the challenges associated with dual diagnosis and, through dedicated training, enable them to respond appropriately to crisis situations specific to individuals with this condition. More importantly, our goal is to foster a preventive approach. To achieve this, we provide a solid theoretical foundation combined with a strong practical orientation, ensuring that participants acquire both the knowledge and the hands-on skills necessary to act effectively in real-life situations. This is accomplished through structured workshops and seminars that bridge theory and practice. • Care, relieve and provide comfort: We strive to alleviate the distress of individuals with a dual diagnosis by offering them a dedicated space-a true laboratory-where they can explore new ways of managing their emotions and interactions in a setting free from immediate social and emotional demands. This environment allows them to develop coping mechanisms and self-regulation strategies without the pressure that often leads to crises. By facilitating this personal and introspective journey, we aim to better equip them to navigate the complexities of the external world with greater resilience and autonomy. Conclusions: Therapeutic workshops significantly mitigate acting-out behaviours, preserving harmony crucial for both patients and mental health professionals.

Title: When the Ward is the Patient: Using the PRISM Protocol to Understand and Reduce Violence in an Inpatient Intellectual Disability Setting
Abstract Note: Background: Violence within inpatient settings is a recognized issue, with higher rates being recorded for intellectual disability services. High levels of violence within these settings have a significantly negative impact on patient care, staff welfare, and organizational functioning. Efforts to manage violence typically focusses on the individual. However, situational risk factors for violence contribute significantly to rates of violence within inpatient settings. These can be identified and modified to reduce violence rates. Addressing both situational and individual risk factors for violence can significantly reduce violence rates within secure settings. Methods: Presentation of an illustrative case study of a ward that experienced high levels of violence results in staff injury, burnout and low morale. Description of the application of the PRISM protocol to identify and address the relevant situational risk factors resulted in demonstrable reductions in violence and improvements in service provision. Results: The case study outlines the practical application of assessing and managing situational risk factors for violence in a locked intellectual disability ward to effectively reduce levels of violent incidents. The presentation will describe the violence and critical issues faced by the ward, with a timeline of events and the impact of the application of the PRISM protocol. Conclusions: The reduction in violence seen in this unit provides 'real world' evidence that addressing situational factors for institutional violence can be effective in intellectual disability inpatient settings, with beneficial outcomes for patients and staff. While individual patient risk assessment and risk management are key components of forensic mental health care, situational risk factors for violence are highly relevant to rates of violence within secure care settings. Structured assessment of situational risk factors should be considered when inpatient settings experience persistent high levels of violence.

Title: Understanding Anxiety and Emotional Outbursts: Insights From Families of People With Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
Abstract Note: Background: People with rare genetic syndromes associated with intellectual disability, including Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RTS), are often at higher risk for anxiety and emotional outbursts than those without rare genetic syndromes. Previous studies suggest that syndrome specific models of anxiety and emotional outbursts can lead to enhanced support for individual groups. In addition, identifying triggers for anxiety in high-risk groups can also help identify targets for intervention to enhance emotional development that cut-across groups. In RTS, preliminary research has indicated that anxiety may change over time, but no research has characterized anxiety or emotional outbursts in detail. This study used a bottom-up interview approach to explore the presentation of anxiety and emotional outbursts in both children and adults with RTS. Methods: Twenty-three parents/carers of individuals with RTS (mean age = 15.28 years, SD = 10.91, range = 6-49; 16 females) completed a structured clinical interview via Microsoft Teams adapted from a published interview developed for intellectual disability research. Questions focused on the emergence and trajectory of anxiety and emotional outbursts, including perceived triggers and age-related changes. Responses were analysed quantitatively. Results: 18 parents reported anxiety to impact their child; most parents reported their child's anxieties to affect their ability to do things the child or family would like to do. The most common immediate triggers were sensory sensitivities (n = 11). Parents reported varied patterns in the onset of anxiety, with emergence occurring in early childhood, mid-childhood or adolescence. Regarding change over time, parents reported anxiety had improved (n = 5) or persisted or worsened (n = 13). 22 parents reported emotional outbursts to impact their child; over half of parent/carers reported an immediate trigger relating to their child not being able to access what they want/need or being restricted in some way (n = 16). The most reported responses were seeing angry emotions daily (n = 8), and behaviours included emotional vocalizations and physical aggression to objects and others. Emotional outbursts were most frequently reported to emerge in early childhood (ages 2-4), with limited communication strategies reported as a key onset trigger (n = 6). Over time, some parents noted improvement (N = 6) in outbursts, but most noted persistence or worsening (N = 15). Conclusions: Findings suggest that anxiety persists over time in RTS, and for some individuals, anxiety early interventions aiming to support day-to-day living skills could be beneficial. The frequency and behaviours associated with emotional outbursts suggest a high level of emotional outburst severity and may be impacting child and family functioning. Several factors identified in the study could be targeted areas of support to reduce anxiety and outburst severity. Identifying shared triggers e could inform broader support strategies.

Title: Moving together: psychomotor family therapy in families with a child with mild intellectual disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: Caregivers of children with mild intellectual disabilities (MID) face various challenges, such as psychological and behavioural issues in the child, leading to dysfunctional family interaction. In Dutch, youth and disability care psychomotor therapy and family therapy have been combined as psychomotor family therapy (PMFT) for many years. However, effectiveness of PMFT in this group has not been studied. Methods: Families with at least one child with MID, experiencing significant parenting challenges, poor communication and a disrupted parent-child relationship, were eligible for PMFT. We studied PMFT's effect on interactions in nine families, as well as experiences with PMFT of family members and care professionals involved. Both quantitative (questionnaires) and qualitative (semi-structured interviews) methods with repeated measurements were used, including questions about behavioural problems, parent-child interaction and experiences with PMFT. Results: Concerning the behavioural problems, no significant differences were found between before and after PMFT. However, the parent-child interaction significantly improved. Thematic analysis of the interview transcripts yielded seven themes about experiences: positive and negative experience, learning through doing, unmet expectations, challenges, obstructive and promoting factors. Additionally, seven themes about effect emerged: behavioural change, changes in family-interaction, acceptance, teamwork, improved parenting, awareness and conflicts. Conclusions: This first pilot study on PMFT suggests that PMFT could be a valuable treatment for families with a child with MID and dysfunctional interactions. Although no effect on behavioural problems was found, this study shows that PMFT seems to have a positive effect on parent-child interaction and helps the family to experience more peace. Experience-based work and having fun together as a family were found to be the key effective factors.

Title: Behavioural and Psychological Symptoms in Dementia in Daily Practice
Abstract Note: Background: The high prevalence of behavioural and psychological symptoms in dementia burdens caregivers of people with intellectual disability and challenges organizations. They require new, specific support methods. Organizations should prepare their staff and families and might reorganize or seek cooperation with dementia experts. We focus on different presentations of BPSD in practice and on the challenges caregivers and organizations meet. Methods: We derived data from our daily work in a service for people with intellectual disability, of whom several have and had dementia; from the stories daily caregivers tell us and the questions they pose on the regular courses we give on dementia in Flanders; from the expertise of the Flemish Centre of Expertise in Dementia; and from scientific research (i.e., our GOUD-Vlaanderen study, KU Leuven). Results: We illustrate, both from practice and from research, different behavioural and psychological symptoms in people with intellectual disability. Memory loss, delusional thinking and hallucinations, lowered or heightened moods, irritability, apathy or aggression, restlessness, difficulties with eating, drinking or sleeping challenge the client, the people living with the client and caregivers. We present some of the challenges for daily caregivers and organizations when confronted with BPSD, and some important guidelines for organizations, derived from the systematic literature review we performed. Conclusions: The challenges caused by (changing) behavioural and psychological symptoms threaten both the well-being of clients and of their caregivers. It is important that caregivers, and if possible also clients, are well informed on these symptoms, on their causes, on the best ways to support these behaviours and to remain well balanced. Training, cooperation with experts and preparing organizations are key.

Title: Keeping Aggressive Behaviour in Check
Abstract Note: Background: Adults with mild intellectual disabilities or borderline intellectual functioning (MID-BIF) are often referred for treatment due to aggressive behaviour. Psychomotor therapy (PMT), a body-and movement-oriented intervention, has shown to be a promising treatment for individuals with MID-BIF exhibiting aggressive behaviour. One pivotal element of PMT, interoceptive awareness (IA), is raising in order to recognize anger, as it is a precursor for aggressive behaviour. Besides that, PMT emphasizes practicing adequate coping skills, as they are crucial to regulate anger. To enhance the quality of PMT in clinical practise, a well-founded standardized psychomotor intervention is recommended. Methods: A psychomotor intervention for adults with MID-BIF exhibiting aggressive behaviour was created following the guidelines for the development of a well-founded intervention program for people with intellectual disabilities/long-term care (Vilans, the Netherlands). This was based on an Intervention Mapping Approach, using scientific literature, experiences of 21 therapists, and experiences of 8 adults with MID-BIF who completed the psychomotor treatment. Results: This research aims to provide a standardized psychomotor intervention for the treatment of aggressive behaviour: Keeping aggressive behaviour in check [Agressie te Lijf]. Key ingredients in the intervention with an experiential character are interoceptive awareness and adequate copings skills. These elements can be practiced using body experiences and movement, in an increasing level of arousal and in an increasing complexity of the context. This led to a framework for therapists for their clinical practice. The framework is founded with theory on body signals and coping skills related to anger and aggressive behaviour. Concrete guidelines for therapists are related to the framework, such as activities, measurement instruments and formats for (homework) assignments. Conclusions: Keeping aggressive behaviour in check [Agressie te Lijf] is recognized by Vilans as a well-founded intervention for people with MID-BIF exhibiting aggressive behaviour. This standardized intervention provides practical and helpful guidlines for application and implementation of this psychomotor intervention in clinical practice and research.

Title: Supporting Persons With Intellectual Disabilities and Mental Health Problems: Findings From the Scientific Literature
Abstract Note: Background: 'Crossbars' and 'The Cross-Linking Network' are two initiatives set up in response to a call from the Flemish Agency for People with Disabilities to find out which support model fits (and works) for intellectually disabled people with very challenging (and escalating) behaviour. The experimental initiatives receive extra resources to set up a model that combines expertise from both specialized mental care health and intellectual disability care. The ultimate aim is that clients will be able, after a period of maximum 4 years, to transfer to a less intensive support programme. Methods: Both initiatives are followed up by Ghent University, Department of Special Needs Education and University College Ghent. In this session, the available scientific knowledge on the support of individuals with 'dual diagnosis' (intellectual disability and mental health problems) will be presented. By means of an explorative search in scientific databases (Web of Science and Medline), review studies and meta-analyses and studies that address international inspiring examples will be summarized. Based on the literature, contact will also be sought with international colleagues who could provide additional input on possible international 'good/inspiring' practices. Results: Based on this literature study and expert consultation, an overview of (international) findings/insights/examples of inspiring practices related to supporting persons with ID and mental health problems will be presented. There will be specifically focused on inspiring treatment and support models and interventions, situated on the micro-, meso-and macro-level (e.g., the IDD paradigm of shared citizenship [Schalock et al. 2022]). Preliminary results point towards the added value of a continuum of care for individuals with intellectual disabilities and co-occurring psychiatric and/or behavioural problems, from residential units to community-based approaches. In Norway, for example, three possibilities for 'linkage' are identified: (1) units for people with intellectual disabilities and mental health problems, (2) formal agreements between services for people with disabilities and mental healthcare within hospitals and (3) tailored care pathways for these individuals within hospitals. These and other examples, as well an overview the findings from the literature, will be presented and discussed.

Title: When a Child Is Violent
Abstract Note: Background: The When a Child is Violent project (2020-2022) was carried out by the Tukena Foundation. The project sought solutions for families in which a child or young person under 25 years of age, with special needs (intellectual disability, autism, ADHD), exhibited violent behaviour towards family members. During the project, it was found that violent behaviour in children and young people with special needs is often linked to stress, insufficient problem-solving skills, and difficulties with emotional regulation. Other underlying factors may include communication difficulties or loneliness. Parents subjected to violence described feelings of guilt, hopelessness, and helplessness. Their children's violent behaviour triggered feelings of fear and shame. Often, parents' fear was also linked to concerns about their own and their other children's safety. Methods: The project used several methods to identify and address violent behaviour in children and young people with special support needs, for example, Self-Regulation Techniques Co-Regulation and Support Strategies for Parents, Crisis and Violence Prevention Techniques. Results: The results showed that violence in families with children with special needs decreased when parents received individualized support and family work focused on managing violent behaviour. However, many parents were completely exhausted and overwhelmed, with their resources severely depleted. Before addressing the child's violent behaviour, it was crucial to first strengthen the parents' emotional resilience and coping abilities, ensuring they had the energy and capacity to support their child effectively. Family safety improved, and peer support provided parents with valuable resources and practical tools for everyday challenges. Additionally, violence within families by children with special needs became a more visible issue, and awareness, as well as professionals' ability to recognize and address experiences related to shame, was strengthened. Conclusions: It is extremely important to talk about violence committed by children and young people. Recognizing violence is the first step towards finding a solution. When families gain the courage to talk about the issue, they can receive support and guidance from professionals. It also helps communities and society to better understand how to support families with a child or young person who behaves violently.

Title: Inclusive PTSD-Treatments for People With ID: Embracing Diversity/Enhancing Talent!
Abstract Note: Background: It is commonly known that people with intellectual disabilities (ID) experience the full range of psychiatric disorders. In most studies, prevalence rates turn out much higher than in the general population. More specifically, adults with an ID are at increased risk for experiencing adverse events, and post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is more prevalent within the ID-population. However, still relatively little is known about evidence-based treatment for PTSD in adults with ID. In addition, diagnostic overshadowing and misdiagnosing are common problems in this population and lead to a lack of adequate treatment of PTSD symptoms. Too often, there is the misconception that people with an ID are not stable enough for PTSD-treatment or that it is not possible to treat PTSD in this population, thus leading to a large group of people with Intellectual disabilities suffering serious complaints that can be treated effectively but are not. One of the important factors in effective PTSD treatment in this specific population is to approach treatment from a multidimensional perspective and have eye for the clients symptoms and (problem-) behaviour and also take into account their cognitive and practical abilities and their emotional developmental level (as described in Anton Dosen's theory). Methods: The speakers in this workshop will present you with an overview of the state of the art knowledge regarding evidence based treatments for adults with ID and PTSD. In addition, they will inform you about adapting earlier stated treatments in order to fit your clients' intellectual level and level of adaptive functioning (conceptual, social and practical). You will learn that every involved professional and informal caregiver is necessary and important in successfully treating PTSD in this population. Participants will be provided with many examples (of successful and less successful trauma-sensitive care) and opportunities to practice with the provided information (e.g., in forms of role-play). There will also be room for debate, exploring different points of view and discussing your own cases. Conclusions: The speakers' final goal is to provide participants with the knowledge they need in order to successfully recognize and (psychologically) treat PTSD in their clients with ID and (complex)PTSD. Furthermore, they aim to inspire and motivate colleagues to start applying the available knowledge, for more clients with PTSD and ID receive the care they need and have a right tot receive. This, in order to provide the population with ID and PTSD with inclusive mental health-and PTSD-care. When we, as (mental) health care-professionals, embrace diversity and enhance our view on trauma (sensitive) treatment, PTSD will not longer stand in the way of clients ability to enhance their talents.

Title: Parents' and Healthcare Professionals' Experiences in Interprofessional Collaboration in Rare Genetic Intellectual Disability Syndrome: A Qualitative Study Into Barriers and Facilitators
Abstract Note: Background: People with rare genetic intellectual disability syndromes (RGIDS) have physical and mental health related problems, with a high risk for challenging behaviour (e.g., aggression and self-injury). They rely on the integrated and specialized expertise of numerous healthcare professionals across medical care, intellectual disability (ID) care, mental care and social care. In addition, parents are often experts in their child's genetic syndrome, health and behavioural issues. They also play a key role in interacting with and connecting the professionals involved in their child's care. However, interprofessional collaboration with parents and multiple healthcare professionals is challenging, especially in the case of RGIDS people living at home. In daily practice, professionals often work in silos, with limited communication and lack of coordination in the care process. While medical issues and genetic diagnosis receive primary attention, parents frequently experience a gap in behavioural care. As a result, parents often find themselves taking on a professional role in addition to being a parent and caregiver, which may not always be within their capabilities. This underscores the need for improved interprofessional collaboration. Therefore, this study explored the barriers and facilitators experienced by parents and healthcare professionals in interprofessional collaboration. Methods: A qualitative approach was used, interviewing parents and healthcare professionals of people with RGIDS and challenging behaviour. All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using the thematic analyses. Data were collected until sufficiency was reached. Results: The results will outline the barriers and facilitators experienced by both parents and healthcare professionals in interprofessional collaboration. As the interviews are currently being conducted and require analysis, the findings are expected to be presented in September 2025. Conclusions: By understanding the barriers and facilitators in interprofessional collaboration (with parents in an expert role), we expect to identify areas for improvement and unravel minimal professional competences to enhance interprofessional collaboration and address what is needed to adequately service and treat families of RGIDS people. This study is designed to hopefully unburden parents, allowing them to collaborate more equally as experts in their child's care.

Title: Preliminary Insights on the AABI-ID: Exploring Caregiver Perspectives on Behavioural Patterns in Adults With ID From an Attachment-Based Perspective
Abstract Note: Background: Attachment behaviours can be defined as behaviours occurring between an individual and a caregiver, aimed at seeking and maintaining proximity and/or protesting separation. These behaviours are thought to regulate fear, anxiety, or other forms of distress in response to real or perceived threats. Although limited, some studies suggest that primary care staff can function as attachment figures for adults with intellectual disabilities (ID), particularly in group home settings. In a previous study (Rinaldi et al., 2023) exploring support workers' representations of attachment behaviours in adults with ID, staff reported a wide range of behavioural manifestations aligning with this definition. The findings underscored support workers' uncertainties regarding the appropriate professional stance to adopt. Notably, no clear distinction emerged between behaviours perceived as a normative form of bonding and those considered problematic. However, this study did not allow for an individual-level analysis of these behaviours, nor did it clarify whether they were expressed selectively or indiscriminately towards support staff. To address these gaps, we developed the Adult Attachment Behaviour Inventory-Intellectual Disabilities (AABI-ID), designed to further explore these findings in greater depth. Additionally, the study aims to position the AABI-ID as a reflective tool, enabling professionals to better understand and respond to the attachment needs of adults with ID, fostering a caregiving dynamic centred on co-regulation and emotional support. Methods: The Adult Attachment Behaviour Inventory- Intellectual Disabilities (AABI-ID) is a third party assessment tool completed by a support worker about an adult with intellectual disabilities (ID) whom they accompany daily. The inventory consists of 22 pairs of items: one item (a) referring to the professional's own experience and one item (b) concerning their observations of the individual's behaviour towards other professionals. Responses are rated on a 7-point Likert scale, based on behavioural observations made by informants who have known the person for at least 6 months. For each participant, the inventory was completed twice (with a maximum interval of 3 weeks) by two informants: an Individual Support Worker (ISW) and an Other Support Worker (OSW). Additionally, the Vineland Adaptive Behaviour Scale (VABS) and the Behaviour Problem Inventory (BPI) were administered to examine the influence of adaptive behaviour and behavioural challenges on attachment behaviours. Results: Preliminary results from data on 103 adults with ID indicate excellent internal consistency of the AABI-ID. Significant positive correlations were found between test and re-test scores for the total AABI-ID, for both ISW and OSW ratings. Additionally, a more clinically focused analysis will be developed to explore the practical implications of using this tool in caregiving contexts. Conclusions: The AABI-ID offers preliminary insights into attachment-related behavioural patterns in adults with ID. It supports professionals in better understanding their clients' needs while encouraging reflection on their own caregiving experiences.

Title: Emotional and Cognitive Responses of Caregivers to Behaviours in Adults With Intellectual Disability: A Standardized Scenario Study
Abstract Note: Background: The well-being of adults with intellectual disabilities (ID) in institutional settings significantly depends on the quality of care provided by direct-care staff. Attachment theory suggests that primary caregivers often act as attachment figures for individuals with ID, highlighting the importance of sensitive and attuned caregiving to address emotional security and distress regulation needs. However, the dynamics between attachment behaviours and the emotional experiences of professionals in such contexts remain underexplored. Previous studies have shown that professionals perceive behaviours linked to attachment and problem behaviours as stress-inducing, with a notable impact on their emotional well-being and caregiving practices. This study investigates how challenging behaviours, including attachment-related and non-attachment- related behaviours, influence professionals' stress, emotional responses, and caregiving strategies within institutional care settings. By examining these interrelations, the research seeks to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the caregiver-client dynamic and its implications for improving care quality. Methods: This study investigates the emotional and cognitive experiences of professionals supporting adults with intellectual disabilities (ID) when exposed to adult's behaviours. Two standardized clinical vignettes were developed and validated by professionals as well as experts' committees: one depicting attachment-related behaviours and the other describing behaviours stemming from alternative causes, such as environmental or learned factors. Participants were randomly assigned the order in which they received the two vignettes and completed validated scales assessing self-efficacy, controllability, and emotional responses for each vignette. The analyses examined main effects (e.g., vignette type) and interactions involving contextual variables such as protocol order, years of professional experience, and staff values. Results: The current preliminary sample consists of 53 direct-care professionals with a mean age of 39.28 years (SD = 12.34) and an average of 14.93 years of professional experience (SD = 11.37). Most participants were identified as female (67.9%) and held either a bachelor's degree (58.5%) or a secondary school diploma (28.3%), with gender and education levels evenly distributed across protocols. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two vignette orders, with 54.7% in Protocol 1 and 45.3% in Protocol 2. Conclusions: These preliminary findings highlight the complex interplay between contextual factors, such as vignette order, and individual differences, like professional values, in shaping caregivers' emotional and cognitive responses to challenging behaviours in institutional care settings. While no significant differences in self-efficacy or controllability were observed between attachment-related and non-attachment- related behaviours, emotional responses, particularly distress and joy, were notably influenced by contextual and individual factors. Data collection is still ongoing, and future analyses with a larger sample will aim to validate these trends and provide deeper insights into the caregiver-client dynamic.

Title: Supporting and Treating (Young) Adults With Dual Diagnosis: Working With Countertransference, Exclusion, and Unmotivated Clients, From an Outreach Team
Abstract Note: Background: Supporting and treating people with intellectual disabilities and mental health issues can be quite complex. Often, they are not very motivated or lose motivation quickly, exhibit aggression causing supporters to feel fear and helplessness, or have tried so many things that they are no longer welcome anywhere. How do you continue working with these people and their network, and where are the opportunities to break the spiral of rejection and powerlessness? Methods: In this symposium, we highlight, through several case studies each focusing on a different aspect of this issue, a number of levers and effective factors. Results: Supporting teams and families in identifying underlying needs and requirements, finding ways to keep returning to clients, and helping to see parallel processes are some effective factors to break the spiral of rejection and powerlessness. Conclusions: This demonstrates that investing in supporting- through coaching-practitioners and supporters who work directly with these (young) adults can make a significant difference in maintaining support and avoiding breakdowns.

Title: Enhancing Emotional Security: A Crucial Step in Hospitalizing Adults With Intellectual Disabilities and Severe Behavioural Disorders
Abstract Note: Background: Treating severe psychiatric and behavioural decompensation in patients with intellectual disabilities (ID) requires a specialized neurobehavioural/psychiatric unit staffed by a highly qualified multidisciplinary team. The population's complex needs require specific expertise due to intellectual functioning challenges, adaptive behaviour limitations, and physical health issues (Schützwohl & Sappok, 2020). Addressing emotional needs is crucial for treating neuropsychiatric disorders and implementing a multidisciplinary approach, especially when behavioural patterns reflect attachment issues. Individuals with ID are at a higher risk of attachment difficulties (Hamadi & Fletcher, 2021). In addition to functional behavioural analysis, attachment theory may also provide useful insights for managing these patients' behaviour (Rinaldi et al., 2022). Can emotional co-regulation and dyadic adaptation serve as therapeutic strategies for behavioural disorders? Can meeting the patient's emotional needs support the multidisciplinary team in the implementation of neuropsychiatric and medical care? Methods: We present a case study of an 18-year- old male with autism spectrum disorder, ID, and severe behavioural disorders. Admitted during an acute behavioural crisis endangering himself and others, his behavioural decompensation emerged amid multiple stressors: his transitioning from paediatric to adult care, a change in residence, his mother's pregnancy announcement, and reduced home visits-all exacerbated by his heightened need for attention. After assessing his emotional development using the Scale of Emotional Development-Short (Meinecke et al., 2024), the team received support recommendations and training. The intervention strategy incorporated continuous support and positive feedback to encourage him. During aggressive episodes, the team maintained engagement through proximity and active communication rather than resorting to withdrawal. Emotional co-regulation techniques were implemented to support the patient in emotional stabilization. Individualized support was prioritized, and during stabilization, he was separated from the group to aid recovery. Small daily goals were set, supported by a token economy system. Additionally, efforts were made to rebuild the bond with the family through two weekly mediated visits with the parents. Results: This approach facilitated relational management of the patient's behaviour, significantly mitigating risks to both himself and others. It allowed for new educational interventions, previously hindered by his aggression, and enabled a thorough medical reassessment of his diagnosis and treatment plan. This case serves to illustrate the implementation of a psycho-educational clinical system based on emotional development and attachment theories. This system aimed to meet the specific emotional needs of the patient, stabilize his behaviour, and improve the multidisciplinary team's care delivery. It has proved to be an essential complement to the patient's comprehensive care plan. Conclusions: Although traditional clinical and behavioural approaches remain essential for patients with attachment difficulties, our clinical case suggests that they may be insufficient without an emphasis on emotional development. The approach used significantly strengthened the patient's emotional and behavioural security, fostering a safe environment for both the patient and the care team. This foundation was crucial for the successful implementation of multidisciplinary healthcare interventions.

Title: Case Study: “He Doesn't Belong Here”
Abstract Note: Background: P is a young man with a moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and complex trauma. He no longer has a biological support network. His professional caregivers describe his behaviour as challenging, including physical aggression, running away, controlling behaviours, and clinginess. He appears to have an insatiable need for closeness and care. The support team wonders whether P truly belongs within their residential group. Would not he be better off living in a closed living group? Methods: The case of P and the support provided to the team will be examined. Results: In supporting teams working with clients like P, we notice that focusing on perception and framing can sometimes be counterproductive. How can we move beyond resistance? What obstacles do we sometimes encounter during outreach processes? Conclusions: This case illustrates the need for and the added value of supporting professional caregivers in providing care for this target group.

Title: We Do not Care Anymore-Do We?! Shift in Support Models for People With DID and Challenging Behaviour
Abstract Note: Background: Individuals with a disorder of intellectual development (DID) and behaviour described as challenging (CB) are particularly vulnerable to violence and restrictive interventions, despite their fundamental human right to be protected from harm. Misunderstood concepts of care and protection may contribute to excessive restrictions of personal autonomy and practices to control behaviour, for example, physical restraint, seclusion, or other coercive methods. The research project “Gemeinschaftlich mit unterstuetzter Teilhabe“(GUT; Supporting Community Participation, Bielefeld University) acts in response to an expert commission report following incidents of violence and excessive use of restrictive measures in group homes for individuals with DID in North Rhine-Westphalia. The commission highlighted a lack of data on the living conditions of the target group. To address this gap, the GUT project applied a mixed-methods approach to examine social relationships, living conditions, employment, health status, and healthcare access for this population in Westphalia. The research project “Network for Intensive Residential Care in Upper Bavaria” (PINO; Munich University) was similarly concerned with the quality of life of people with DID and CB, targeting residents of intensive care units in Upper Bavaria. One of the main objectives was to develop a scientifically based, sustainable core concept for intensive care living that ensures social inclusion in line with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Methods: The workshop will critically discuss barriers and solutions to the social inclusion of a highly vulnerable population, moving away from traditional notions of 'care' towards concepts of supporting autonomy and self-determination. Methods from systemic counselling and design thinking will facilitate a participatory and co-productive exchange of ideas and experience. The integration of perspectives from experts by experience will play a special role. A case vignette will be used to reflect on professional attitudes and strategies in relation to self-determination and protection from violence. Empirical findings from both research projects will be integrated to enrich the discussion. Results: PINO has identified 12 quality standards for improving the living situation of people with DID and CB, including housing concepts, social inclusion as well as professionalization of staff with regard to attitudes and strategies in dealing with CB. Initial results of the project GUT indicate no differences in the idea of self-determination between professionals and clients; however, its realization is limited by structural constraints. The workshop aims to broaden the discourse on self-determination and protective measures in cross-national contexts. By reflecting on attitudes and policies, participants will explore how autonomy and protective interventions can be reconciled. Conclusions: The insights from the workshop will be synthesized into practical recommendations. The focus is on a support model that promotes participatory approaches with regard to violence prevention and social inclusion.

Title: Case Study: “Stealing and Lying, That Crosses My Personal Boundaries!”
Abstract Note: Background: C, a man with a mild intellectual disability and behavioural problems, has a significant impact on his environment. He lives in a nursing home that, with limited resources and expertise, still tries to work with him. They seem to be completely stuck with his behaviour: He enters other people's rooms, steals personal belongings, and smears faeces in rooms and toilets. The original request from the team was to admit him residentially and only let him return once he was treated for these problems. However, through the support of the outreach team, they gradually gained insight into the meaning of C's behaviour and ideas on how to handle it. Methods: This case study shows how the careful introduction of expertise and giving meaning to behaviour can make it understandable and provide actionable insights even in non-specialized contexts. Results: Understanding the underlying causes of his behaviour and identifying the needs that must be met to reduce tension and increase calm helped the team members manage this man. Conclusions: This process demonstrates how behaviour that initially seems insurmountable and is rejected can become understandable and manageable through a specific hypothesis.

Title: How to Provide High-Quality Appropriate Care for People With Mild ID: PSMs as Part of the Solution
Abstract Note: Background: Care and support for people with ID are becoming more and more complex. Additionally, there are more financial pressure and difficulties with finding eligible staff. In order to still provide high-quality appropriate care, psychosocial support methods (PSMs) can help to tackle social, health and psychological challenges faced by people with ID and their caregivers. However, residential facilities face a dilemma which PSM to choose and implement because there is a lack of information, evidence and inconsistency in findings on different PSMs. To date, there is no comprehensive overview of PSMs for people with ID. This study therefore aims to provide this overview of available PSMs as well as their evidence for effectiveness in daily practice. In order to provide this overview this study addresses the following research questions: • What defines a PSM? • Which PSMs are available in Dutch ID healthcare? • How effective and suitable are the PSMs found? Methods: A coherent definition of a PSM was missing. Therefore, we first composed a definition for PSM to standardize terminology and allow appropriate comparison. The definition and benefits of a PSM were addressed by systematically reviewing scientific and grey literature. Both English and Dutch papers were reviewed to establish if the interventions addressed in the papers were indeed meeting our definition of a PSM. If so, we would then search the literature for scientific evidence and practical implementations to support this PSM. Results: A comprehensive literature review was conducted by searching for both English and Dutch scientific and grey literature. After reviewing all papers, 28 interventions met our definition of PSM and were included in this study. Consequently, we checked these PSMs for efficacy and suitability. Based on our criteria for efficacy and suitability, we included 8 PSMs for people with mild intellectual disabilities (MID) and five PSMs for people with MID and severe behavioural problems. After additional review of the included PSMs, Active Support and Triple-C were chosen as the preferred PSMs for people with MID and people with MID and severe behavioural problems, respectively. Conclusions: This study provides an in-depth analysis and synthesis of the body of knowledge about PSMs studied among people with (mild) ID. As such, it has important implications for these individuals, professional caregivers, family members and care organizations. However, there is a long way to go regarding (scientific) evidence of long-term efficacy.
