Title: Trauma in People With Intellectual Disabilities: EMDR Therapy and Care for Support Professionals
Abstract Note: Background: People with intellectual disability (ID) or borderline intellectual functioning (BIF) are at increased risk of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, research into effective trauma treatment remains limited, and it is important to assess the effectiveness of trauma-focused treatments. Therefore, we present two studies that investigated the effectiveness of eye movement and desensitization (EMDR) therapy in individuals with ID. The first study investigated the safety and effectiveness of brief intensive EMDR therapy, delivered by a rotating team of therapists, for adults with MID-BIF, including those with severe behavioural problems. Because people with severe ID (SID) rarely receive trauma treatment due to a lack of knowledge about PTSD treatment options for this population, a second study examined the effectiveness of EMDR therapy using the storytelling method for three adults with SID and PTSD. In addition to people with ID, direct support professionals (DSPs) are at risk of experiencing workplace trauma, such as exposure to challenging behaviour, as part of their daily work. However, little is known about the psychological impact, particularly the traumatic impact, of workplace trauma on DSPs. The psychological well-being of DSPs is important because DSPs are vital for continuous care and their quality of support depends on their well-being. That is why we present a study that assessed the psychological impact of workplace trauma on DSPs of people with ID. Methods: The different studies used a variety of methods including randomized non-concurrent multiple baseline between-subject designs, a scoping review and an online survey. Results: The results of the safety and effectiveness of brief intensive EMDR therapy, carried out by a team of rotating therapists, specifically for adults with MID-BIF and concomitant severe behavioural problems will be presented. Results of the effectiveness of EMDR using the storytelling method in three adults with severe ID and PTSD showed a significant decrease in PTSD symptoms, challenging behaviours and most dysfunctional behaviours. There seems to be an association between workplace trauma in DSPs of people with ID and burn-out, secondary traumatic stress (STS) and/or PTSD. Research on this topic is lacking. The results of an online survey completed by DSPs asking questions about experienced workplace trauma and psychological consequences such as burn-out, secondary traumatic stress (STS), compassion fatigue/satisfaction and/or PTSD symptoms will be presented. Conclusion: EMDR therapy is feasible and effective for people with ID. Support for DSPs of people with ID is important as DSPs may experience mental health problems following workplace trauma.

Title: Brief Intensive EMDR Therapy for PTSD in Adults With Mild Intellectual Disability and Behavioural Problems
Abstract Note: Background: Because individuals with mild intellectual disability or borderline intellectual functioning (MID-BIF) are at an elevated risk of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), it is important to test the effectiveness of trauma-focused treatments, such as eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (EMDR) therapy, including for adults with MID-BIF and severe behavioural problems. The aim of this study is to determine the safety and effectiveness of brief intensive EMDR therapy, carried out by a team of rotating therapists, specifically for adults with MID-BIF. This will provide valuable insights into the potential of trauma-focused interventions for this vulnerable group and help improve treatment options. Methods: Using a randomized non-concurrent multiple baseline between-subject design, 11 adults with MID-BIF and severe behavioural problems received a maximum of 16 intensive EMDR sessions twice daily for a maximum of 2 weeks from six different EMDR therapists. Primary outcome measurements included severity of PTSD symptoms, PTSD diagnostic status and adverse events. Secondary outcome measurements included the frequency and severity of behavioural problems, presence of adaptive behaviour and the use of involuntary care. Outcome measurements were assessed at baseline, during the intervention and post-intervention phases and at the follow- up phases and subject to randomization tests for statistical significance. Results: The results will be presented at the congress. Conclusions: Although the results of this study will be presented at the congress, we can already conclude that it is possible to apply brief intensive EMDR therapy, carried out by a team of rotating therapists, as an intervention for adults with MID-BIF and severe behavioural problems.

Title: The Need for Interprofessional Collaboration in the Care of Individuals With Rare Genetic Intellectual Disability: A Patient Journey Mapping Study
Abstract Note: Background: People with rare genetic intellectual disability syndromes (RGIDS) have physical and mental health related problems, with a high risk for challenging behaviour (e.g., aggression and self-injury). Their care requires long-term complex care involving multiple healthcare professionals. Parents play a key role in coordinating and interacting with these professionals. This study aimed to explore parents' journey with the healthcare system, the networks they have built, and their perceptions of interactions with healthcare professionals over time. Methods: A qualitative approach was used, interviewing parents of people with RGIDS and challenging behaviour. All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Data were collected until sufficiency was reached. Findings were visualized using Patient Journey Mapping. Results: Among the 13 parents interviewed, most described their journey as beginning with concerns about their child's early development. When voicing these concerns, some parents felt unheard by their general practitioner or paediatrician. For some, obtaining specialized care and ultimately receiving a diagnosis was only made possible through their own persistence- navigating a journey filled with referrals, extensive testing, diagnoses, and well-intentioned yet often ill-suited advice on challenging behaviours that did not align with daily life. In terms of their care network, physicians from the medical domain dominated the journey, while behavioural specialists and psychiatrists were rarely involved. This added to parents' ongoing uncertainty and frustration, as their child's challenging behaviours remained unaddressed and impacting their daily life. Also, the lack of interprofessional coordination led to parents' wish for a single point of contact and coordination of proper care. Conclusions: Due to a lack of guidance, people with RGIDS were rarely seen by behavioural professional or psychiatrists, despite numerous consults with medical healthcare professionals. Parents were left to lead the care process themselves, with much of the focus placed on physical problems. This highlights the need for better collaboration and coordination between medical and behavioural professionals to ensure high quality, person-centered care.

Title: EMDR in Three Adults With Severe Intellectual Disability and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder: A Multiple-Baseline Evaluation
Abstract Note: Background: Research on trauma treatment in people with severe ID (SID; IQ 20-35) is scarce and controlled studies are lacking. Although people with SID can suffer severely in response to traumatic events, trauma treatment is rarely provided. This may be explained by challenges in PTSD assessment in people with SID due to their severe verbal and cognitive impairments. Also, there seems to be lack of knowledge of PTSD treatment options for people with SID. This study examined the effectiveness of EMDR using the storytelling method in three adults with severe ID and PTSD. Methods: A multiple-baseline design was used to examine the effects on PTSD classification, PTSD symptoms, challenging behaviours and dysfunctional behaviours in three adults with SID and PTSD. Weekly measurements of PTSD symptoms were administered during baseline, intervention, post-intervention and 3-month- follow- up phases using the DITS-SID, a clinical interview to classify PTSD in persons with severe ID according to DSM-5 PTSD ≤ 6 years criteria. Also, multiple weekly measurements of the frequency of dysfunctional behaviours were taken. To assess challenging behaviours, the BPI was completed three times. Results: EMDR resulted in a significant decrease in PTSD symptoms, challenging behaviours and most dysfunctional behaviours. None of the participants had a PTSD classification after EMDR. No negative side effects were reported, and treatment was not stopped prematurely. Conclusions: The results suggest that EMDR storytelling is a promising treatment option in persons with SID and PTSD symptoms. It is important to include a possible underlying PTSD in understanding and treating challenging behaviours such as self-injury and aggression. Follow-up research with a larger sample size is required.

Title: The Psychological Impact of Workplace Trauma on Direct Support Professionals of People With ID
Abstract Note: Background: Exposure to workplace trauma (i.e., direct and indirect exposure to single and/or multiple traumatic or stressful events and repeated exposure to aversive details of such events) has a psychological impact on mental health professionals such as general distress, burn-out or traumatic symptomology associated with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) or secondary traumatic stress (STS). At an organizational level, the effects of workplace trauma often lead to increased absenteeism, reduced productivity and higher staff turnover, with significant consequences for the quality of care. Direct support professionals (DSPs) are essential in the continuity of care for people with intellectual disabilities (ID), and the quality of their support partly depends on the DSPs' emotional well-being. DSPs are at risk of experiencing workplace trauma as part of their daily work as people with ID show more challenging behaviour and are at greater risk of experiencing traumatic and stressful events than people without ID. Research on the psychological impact of workplace trauma, particularly the traumatic effects, in DSPs of people with ID is scarce. Further research is needed to enable organizational initiatives to understand and minimize the psychological impact of workplace trauma on DSPs and to ensure continuity and quality of care. Methods: First, we conducted a scoping review in accordance with the JBI methodology for scoping reviews and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). Second, using a survey, we inventoried what DSPs of people with ID and challenging behaviour experienced in terms of the extent and types of workplace trauma. We also explored what they experienced in terms of compassion satisfaction, compassion fatigue, PTSD symptoms, STS and burn-out as a result of these events. Results: The scoping review aimed to explore the research question: 'Is workplace trauma in DSPs of people with ID associated with burn-out, STS, compassion fatigue and/or PTSD?' Twenty-one studies were included. The incidence of workplace trauma was high; 50%-90% of the DSPs experienced (daily) aggressive behaviour, and approximately 83% of the DSPs experienced challenging behaviour. Workplace trauma was associated with burn-out. Only four studies focused on the association between workplace trauma and PTSD and STS and showed an association between workplace trauma and PTSD and STS in DSPs of people with ID. The aim of the second study is: 'What are the psychological consequences of workplace trauma in DSPs of people with ID?' The results of the second study are not yet available as the study is ongoing. The results will be presented at the congress. Conclusions: DSPs of people with ID appear to be frequently exposed to workplace trauma such as aggressive and challenging behaviour. As a result, DSPs are at risk of developing mental health problems such as burn-out, PTSS and STS.

Title: How the Sensory Garden Helps in the Regulation of Arousal in Children, Teenagers and Young Adults with Autism, Intellectual Disability and Behavioural Problems
Abstract Note: Background: GAUZZ (centrum voor Gedragsstoornissen bij Autisme en Zware Zorgbehoevendheid) focuses on the treatment of children and young adults between 6 and 25 with autism, intellectual disability and behavioural problems. GAUZZ is a partnership between the Psychiatric Hospital Multiversum and the University Psychiatric Centre KU Leuven. The residential and outreach teams closely work together. Our aim is to increase our patients quality of life, to reduce the behavioural problems and to help strengthen the network around our children and young adults. We try to zoom in on how the patient is functioning and what is needed to optimize this. The sensory garden offers many opportunities to observe a patient but also to discover ways in which they can regulate. Methods: We want to reflect on how a sensory garden provides a treasure of information and how the sensory garden can influence the 'Window of Tolerance' of an individual. Zooming in on how we use it at GAUZZ and why a sensory garden is a very useful tool. Results: We want to highlight the effects a sensory garden can have on the Window of Tolerance. During this symposium, we will share how we transfer the information we get from the sensory garden to the network of our children and young adults. Conclusions: The sensory garden offers many chances in the treatment of the children and young adults of GAUZZ. We hope to inspire family and caregivers to observe and gather valuable information from sensory gardens.

Title: Implementing and Adapting the Multi-Disciplinary Expertise Team Method to Reduce Involuntary Care
Abstract Note: Background: In the Netherlands, the new Care and Coercion Act in 2020 required intellectual disability care organizations to implement new methods that aim to increase clients' self-determination and reduce involuntary care practices. Involuntary care is defined as care provided without clients' consent. The Multi-Disciplinary Expertise Team (MDET) method is a multi-component method that creates awareness among care professionals concerning application of involuntary care and results in advices on reducing involuntary care. MDET proved effective in phasing out involuntary care measures in a previous trial. The current study examined how organizations adapted MDET during implementation and tested whether these versions were also effective. Methods: Four organizations implemented MDET in a way that they felt suited their existing working structures. To describe adaptations made to MDET during implementation, semi-structured interviews with MDET-coordinators were analysed. A quasi-experimental interrupted time-series design tested change in weekly counts of digital involuntary care recordings from before to during MDET implementation, in care homes that implemented MDET (n = 22) compared to care homes providing care-as- usual (CAU). Results: All organizations adapted the MDET method to fit into their work structure and to comply with care professionals' needs. Adaptations varied per organization. These included implementing MDET without an independent MDET-team, reducing the number of care team professionals involved in discussions, and loosening recordings of involuntary care. No differential changes in recordings were found before and after implementing MDET, nor between the implementation-and CAU-groups. Conclusions: Being able to adapt multi-component methods such as MDET was theorized as beneficial in implementation processes, as this would allow organizations to tailor these methods to specific contexts. However, the current study suggested that these adaptions of MDET may have undermined its effects on reducing involuntary care. When implementing such multi-component methods, the efforts of care organizations to change existing work structures may be necessary to contribute to expected objectives and outcomes of these methods.

Title: Effectiveness of a Multidisciplinary Expertise Team in Reducing Restrictive Measures and Involuntary Care
Abstract Note: Background: In line with de UN Convention on the rights of people with disabilities and in preparation for the new Care and Coercion Act (2020), the Multidisciplinary Expertise Team (MDET) method was developed between 2015 and 2019 within a large care organization in the Netherlands. MDET aims to minimize restrictive measures and involuntary care to promote self-determination for people with intellectual disabilities. Involuntary care is defined as care provided without clients' consent. This study assesses the efficacy of the MDET method in reducing such involuntary care measures within Dutch residential care homes for people with intellectual disabilities. Methods: MDET is a multicomponent method leading to a consultation plan with evidence-based advices concerning the reduction of restrictive measures and involuntary care. A clustered randomized trial encompassed 30 residential units, reporting 428 measures on 107 residents through an organization-wide digital registration system. Care homes were randomly assigned to the MDET method or care-as- usual. Results: Care homes assigned to MDET reported a significant stronger reduction (40%) in restrictive measures and involuntary care compared to the care homes working on reduction themselves (care-as- usual, 20%). Conclusions: MDET shows promise in decreasing restrictive measures and involuntary care by enhancing awareness among care professionals concerning involuntary care practices and sharing expertise across disciplines at staff and resident levels.

Title: The Antipsychotic Withdrawal Study: A Randomized Placebo Controlled Trial Investigating Reasons for Failure
Abstract Note: Background: Antipsychotic withdrawal often fails in adults with intellectual disabilities (ID) and challenging behaviour. We aimed to investigate why and proposed three possible mechanisms for antipsychotic withdrawal failure: (1) the influence of caregivers' and family members' subjective interpretations of the behavioural symptoms; (2) the beneficial effects of AP treatment on undiagnosed psychiatric illness, through improvements in sleep or direct effects on behaviour; and (3) the misinterpretation of withdrawal symptoms as a recurrence of challenging behaviour. Methods: A multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized antipsychotic withdrawal trial with a non-inferiority design was conducted, in collaboration with the Academic Collaborative Research Center Healthy Ageing and Intellectual Disabilities. In the withdrawal group (n = 43), antipsychotics were reduced by 25% every 4 weeks, while the control group (n = 42) maintained their dose. The primary outcome was the premature unblinding of the randomization code. If antipsychotics have no effect and subjective expectations from caregivers, adults with ID, and family influence withdrawal, the success and failure rates should be similar in both groups. Therefore, differences in premature unblinding between the withdrawal and control groups were assessed using risk difference and Cox proportional hazards models. The secondary outcomes were psychiatric disorders (ADAMS, PAS-ADD), sleep problems (actigraphy), behavioural issues (ABC, VAS, CGI), and withdrawal symptoms (ADAMS, PAS-AD, MEDS, SHRS, BARS, actigraphy, physical measurements). Differences between groups and over time were analysed using linear mixed models and generalized estimating equations. Results: In the withdrawal group, 15 participants were prematurely unblinded compared to 3 participants in the control group. There was a significant risk difference of 28%, indicating a higher chance of early unblinding in the withdrawal group. Analyses showed that anxiety and depressive mood were significantly higher in the failed withdrawal group compared to the control group. Additionally, behavioural problems significantly increased and the sleep-wake rhythm became less stable over time in the failed withdrawal group. No evidence was found suggesting that withdrawal symptoms contributed to the AP withdrawal failure. Conclusions: In conclusion, AP withdrawal failure cannot (only) be explained by the subjective expectations and interpretation of behaviour of those around the patient or temporary withdrawal symptoms. The onset of anxiety problems, depressive symptoms, behavioural problems, and sleep-wake rhythm disturbances seemed to be the main reasons for AP withdrawal failure in adults with ID and challenging behaviour.

Title: Restrictive Interventions in Intellectual Disability Care: A Study of Legal Compliance and Practice
Abstract Note: Background: The use of restrictive interventions in care services for individuals with intellectual disabilities in Norway has been regulated by a special law since 1999. Restrictive interventions must be documented in pre-approved coercion decisions issued by the County Governor, who holds supervisory responsibility for the service. Decisions can be issued for a maximum of 1 year at a time. The law establishes educational requirements for personnel authorized to implement restrictive interventions, although municipalities may apply for exemptions from these requirements. Aims: This article aims to investigate the use of formalized restrictive interventions in individuals with intellectual disabilities in municipal care services and to examine how the application of restrictive practice aligns with the intent of the legislation in certain areas. Methods: In this cross-sectional study, individuals with intellectual disabilities and coercion decisions from municipalities in Northern Norway were included. Data collection was conducted through semi-structured interviews, validated questionnaires and a review of hospital records and coercion decisions. The primary informants were municipal care providers with in-depth knowledge of the participants and, in some cases, family members. Results: Seventy individuals (73% of eligible) were included, with an average age of 44 years. There is a predominance of individuals with severe and profound intellectual disabilities (77%). The proportion of individuals with genetic syndromes (31%) and autism spectrum disorders (23%) is high. Municipalities apply for exemptions from the educational requirements for personnel in 97% of cases when seeking coercion decisions, and the County Governor grants these requests almost without exception (97%), whereas on-site supervision is rare. The median number of staff in the care services last week was 8 (range 2-28). Staff stability is reported to be low in 23% of cases. Additionally, 29% of participants did not have a valid coercion decision at the time of the study, and many experienced prolonged periods without valid decisions. Conclusions: There is a gap between the practice of restrictive interventions in municipal care services and the wording of the law. To ensure the legal protection of individuals with intellectual disabilities, compliance with the law must be improved, and the competence of service providers implementing restrictive interventions must be enhanced to meet the standards set by the legislation. More frequent supervision of the service is also recommended to ensure professional accountability.

Title: The Use of the Self Harm Scale in Mental Healthcare in Patients With Intellectual Disabilities in the Netherlands
Abstract Note: Background: Even though self-harm and aggression are known to occur in patients with an intellectual impairment, little is known about prevalence in clinical mental health care. Also, little is known about the severity and the impact on daily mental health care. We aimed to investigate which patients experienced incidents at least once and more than four times, as well as the most prevalent diagnoses. We also wanted to know the effects on nurses and staff by using the SHS. Methods: We used the Self-Harm Scale (SHS). We investigated the physical context of the self-harm incident. We then investigated the characteristics of the patient group as a whole and those of the patients who self-harmed most frequently. We started interviewing nurses and staff about their experience with the SHS. Results: Between May 2023 and December 2024, 126 patients were admitted 169 times. A total of 69 incidents occurred. 51 (74%) of these incidents occurred in patients showing between 7 and 19 incidents. These frequently self-harming patients showed significantly more diagnoses of PTSD (chi-square = 5.7, p = 0.015) and autism (chi-square = 5.9, p = 0.028). Self-harm as a whole occurred more in patients with a psychotic disorder (chisquare = 4.29, p + 0.038), also PTSD (chi-square = 5.8, p = 0.017) and a personality disorder (chi-square = 8.7, p = 0.003). The incidents almost all occurred in the patient's room when the patient was alone. Injuries mainly happened at the head, arms and legs. Conclusions: Most of the incidents occurred not in the company of others, especially the severe incidents, which also typically occurred in those showing the most self-harm incidents. Over time, the number of incidents decreased. An important observation is that PTSD, autism, personality and a psychotic disorder are related to more incidents in a patient. Finally, it is worth noting that in 2025, fewer incidents occurred, whether this is a coincidence or due to more awareness and knowledge of how to deal with self-harm. The most positive effect mentioned by nurses and staff is the fact that they are more aware of the topic and feel more secure in dealing with it.

Title: Perspective of the Increased Number of People With ID Treated With Restraint Measures in Norway
Abstract Note: Background: Restraint and restrictive practices are stigmatizing, have a significant negative impact on the quality of life of people with ID and can cause injuries as well as on staff well-being. Restrictive and coercive interventions are common in services for people with ID, and reducing the use of restraints is crucial due to their severe impact on quality of life. A paradoxical increase in the use of planned/legal restraint measures for individuals with intellectual disabilities in Norway has been registered after the introduction of a law intended to limit such practices (Søndenaa et al. 2015). Survey data from caregivers explored the reasons for this increase. Results suggest that heightened awareness of regulations and previous underreporting as key factors. Methods: A cohort study was designed to identify the perspectives of professionals who were involved in the application of restraint measures. Following these perspectives over a decade and comparing two similar cohorts were also an objective. A total of 457 direct care staff members participated in this survey. Of these, 189 were interviewed in 2013 and 268 in 2024. Results: Over the period of 12 years from 2012 to 2024, we noticed some changes in the cohort. Using a chi-square test, the proportion of men had increased from 24.7% to 35.8% (X (1) = 6.29, p = 0.012), and the proportion of nursing staff (bachelor's degree) had increased from 39.7% to 49.6% (X(2) = 6.67, p = 0.036). Non-significant changes were found in queries of experience, restraint knowledge, practical implications related to restraint measures and the suggestion of unreported restraint measures. Conclusions: More details will be presented.

Title: Exploring the Adaptive Functioning and Psychiatric Phenotype in Children and Adults With Dravet Syndrome
Abstract Note: Background: Dravet syndrome (DS) is a rare genetic epilepsy syndrome, causing refractory seizures, delayed development, intellectual disability, and behavioural difficulties. The reported prevalence of behavioural difficulties in DS ranges between 37% and 100%. However, in-depth psychiatric phenotyping is lacking. Thus, this study aims to explore and describe the developmental profile of children and adults with Dravet syndrome, including adaptive functioning and psychiatric symptoms using a combination of questionnaires, a structured interview completed with parents, and an in-person clinical assessment of individuals with DS. Methods: We collected data from questionnaires completed by parents, used data on patient characteristics from our previous studies and performed an in-person clinical assessment during a home visit with the participant and their parent(s). The following measures were completed: the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule 2nd edition (ADOS-2), the Psychiatric Assessment Schedule for Adults with Developmental Disabilities (Mini PAS-ADD), the Child Behaviour Checklist (CBCL) 1.5-5 years and 6-18 years and the Adult Behaviour Checklist 18-59 years (ABCL), the social responsive scale second edition (SRS-2) and social responsive scale adult version (SRS-A), the behaviour problems inventory (BPI) and the adaptive behaviour assessment system, third edition (ABAS-3). Results: Sixty-five individuals with DS took part in the study, with 47 participating in the home visit. The median age of participants was 16 years (range: 2-45), and the majority (n = 29, 44.6%) had a severe intellectual disability (IQ < 30). Individuals with DS exhibit an overall very low adaptive functioning, impaired social skills, autistic traits and a high prevalence of other psychiatric symptoms like self-injurious behaviour, aggressive/ destructive behaviour, stereotyped behaviour and attention problems. Older DS individuals tend to show lower adaptive functioning and more autistic traits compared to younger DS individuals, although these differences are not statistically significant. Furthermore, individuals with more pronounced autistic traits often present with a more severe overall DS phenotype. Conclusions: DS individuals show a behavioural pattern characterized by an increasing discrepancy with age-required norms, often described as 'growing into deficit'. The knowledge on this behavioural phenotype among DS individuals could facilitate the development of tailored behavioural and (para)medical approaches, which may improve also the quality of life of DS individuals and their parents.

Title: Reducing Caregiver Stress Through a Mentalization-Based Support training
Abstract Note: Background: Persons with intellectual disabilities often have behavioural problems such as stereotypies, aggression and violence, which can result in self-injury, harm to others or destruction of property (Smith and Matson 2010). This behaviour is not only harmful to themselves but also poses a challenge for their (professional) caregivers. Stressed caregivers engage in fewer interactions with clients, display more negative and fewer positive interactions, and behave in ways that contribute to maintaining challenging behaviour and stress in individuals with intellectual disabilities (Simons et al. 2021). Mentalizing can be defined as the ability to understand one's own and others' behaviour in terms of underlying mental states such as feelings, desires, and beliefs (Bateman and Fonagy 2006). It is essential for caregivers to adopt a mentalizing stance (Fonagy 2004), which means remaining flexible and tolerant, even in challenging situations. To support caregivers in developing mentalizing skills, the mentalization-based support training was developed. This study focuses on examining the effectiveness of this training in reducing stress among caregivers. Methods: The mentalization-based support (MBS) training is based on a psychoeducational approach, in which participants receive information on mentalizing in daily practice and consists of three half-day sessions, a total study load of approximately 24 h. Participants (N = 100: 76 female; 24 male) were caregivers providing support to persons with an intellectual disability in group-home facilities in the Netherlands. The caregivers completed the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-14) and an adapted 20-item Social Validity Scale, both using a 5-point Likert scale. A baseline measurement (T0) was performed at the start of the intervention, and a second measurement (T1) after completing the intervention. Results: Of the 100 participants, 59% completed the second measurement. No significant effects were found on perceived stress between the baseline measurement and the second measurement. When looking at the individual items on the Social Validity Scale, participants said they noticed improvements in their mentalizing skills and being more aware of their own emotions. Conclusions: The effect of MBS-training on perceived stress of caregivers remains uncertain. As participants reported that the training was instructive and contributed to understanding their own needs and those of their clients, it is recommended to improve the training and examine the effects.

Title: Emotional Development, Mental Health and Challenging Behaviour
Abstract Note: Background: This symposium explores the dynamic nature of emotional development (ED) and its significance in psychiatric diagnostics and interventions. The Scale of Emotional Development-Short (SED-S) serves as a valuable tool for assessing the level of ED and thereby helps to distinguish between developmentally (appropriate) behaviour and symptoms for mental illnesses. Understanding a person's level of ED supports to determine whether behaviours stem from a mismatch between emotional needs and the environmental expectations/tasks or indicate an additional psychiatric disorder. However, ED is not a fixed construct; it is influenced by internal factors such as psychiatric conditions and external influences like major life events. This symposium highlights the dynamic nature of the emotional development approach and its implications for clinical practice. Methods/Results: Tanja Sappok presents a longitudinal and cross-sectional study on the relationship between depressive episodes and the level of emotional development. The second presentation from Romina Rinaldi focuses on the connection between the level of emotional development and challenging behaviours, exploring individual profiles, assessments and tailored support strategies. Carlos Peña-Salazar examined the impact of the level of ED in individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID), analysing how neuropsychiatric disorders and problem behaviours relate to the emotional development of a person. The final presentation from Marco Montanari investigates the correlation between emotional development, empathy and embodied expression in adults with ID. A pretest-posttest study over 8 months, using SED-S and a test measuring emotional involvement in autism, aims to validate the hypothesis that ED, empathy and embodied expression are deeply interconnected. Conclusions: This symposium is highly relevant for clinicians, researchers and practitioners in psychiatric and psychological fields, as it provides insights into how the diagnostics of emotional developmental can inform psychiatric practice, enhance individualized interventions and contribute to a better understanding of behavioural expressions in individuals with ID and related conditions.

Title: Exploring the Role of Creative Arts Therapies, Psychomotor Therapy and Play Therapy in Stress Management for People With Severe Intellectual Disabilities: A Concept Mapping Study
Abstract Note: Background: People with severe intellectual disabilities (ID) face significant challenges in communicating their emotions and needs, leaving them vulnerable to heightened stress and resulting in behaviours such as self-injury, aggression, and compulsive actions. Traditional stress management approaches, which often rely on verbal communication and introspection, are unsuitable for this population. Non-verbal, experience-based therapies- such as Creative Arts Therapies (CATs), psychomotor therapy, and play therapy-offer promising alternatives. These therapies use movement, music, play, and other sensory-based elements to facilitate emotional expression, self-regulation, and stress relief. However, limited research exists on which therapeutic elements are most effective in stress reduction for people with severe ID. Methods: This study employed a concept mapping approach to systematically identify key elements within CATs, psychomotor therapy, and play therapy that contribute to stress reduction. Data were collected through five online focus groups involving 39 stakeholders, including relatives (n = 8), direct support staff (n = 6), creative arts therapists (n = 8), practitioners (n = 11), and managers (n = 6). Participants generated, sorted, and rated statements regarding how music, movement, and play support stress management in individuals with severe ID. The resulting data were analysed using multidimensional scaling and hierarchical cluster analysis to create concept maps reflecting consensus across stakeholder groups. Results: Preliminary analysis identified key themes that contribute to stress reduction in people with severe ID, as reported by various stakeholder groups. Emerging overarching themes include connection through nonjudgmental recognition and being seen and heard, as well as positive experiences that foster a sense of capability through enjoyable, accessible activities aligned with individual interests. A sensitive and responsive therapeutic approach enhances mutual engagement and reciprocity, while distraction and grounding in the present reduce stress by using materials or movement as shared focal points. Adaptation and flexibility allow for individualized adjustments in rhythm, tone, and intensity to meet sensory and emotional needs, while structure and predictability provide security through recognizable patterns, rhythm, and clear transitions. Regulation through bodily sensations, such as movement and sound, supports stress reduction by stimulating or calming individuals and reducing reliance on verbal expression for emotional regulation. As these themes are still being refined, the final overarching themes will be presented at the conference, further substantiated by ongoing analysis. Conclusions: Findings emphasize the importance of integrating non-verbal, sensory-based approaches into stress management interventions for people with severe ID. Effective implementation requires both structured therapeutic frameworks and the flexibility to adapt to individual needs. These insights provide a foundation for optimizing CATs, psychomotor therapy, and play therapy interventions, ensuring their relevance and impact in intellectual disability care.

Title: Emotional Development and Challenging Behaviours: Profiles, Assessments and Tailored Support Strategies
Abstract Note: Background: Challenging behaviours (CB) represent a critical issue in the support of adults with intellectual disabilities (ID). However, distinguishing CB from clinical manifestations of mental health disorders remains complex, particularly in individuals with diverse cognitive and emotional profiles. Recent studies highlight the role of emotional development (ED), assessed using tools such as the Scale of Emotional Development-Short (SED-S), as a key factor in understanding the interplay between ID, CB and psychiatric comorbidities. These findings indicate that delays or heterogeneous ED profiles are associated with an increased prevalence of CB and a higher likelihood of inappropriate psychotropic treatments. This underscores the importance of integrating ED assessment into diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to enhance quality of life and promote social inclusion. This study aims to further explore the associations between emotional development, as measured by the French version of the SED-S, and challenging behaviours in individuals with ID, with particular attention to the role of co-occurring mental health diagnoses in shaping these behaviours. Methods: Participants included 129 adults with mild to profound intellectual disability (ID), recruited from residential and clinical settings in Belgium and Switzerland. Associations between emotional development levels, assessed using the French version of SED-S, and the frequency of challenging behaviours, measured with the Behaviour Problem Inventory, were examined. The influence of mental disorders on stereotyped, self-injurious and aggressive behaviours was evaluated using cumulative models adjusted for ID severity, as well as interaction models accounting for emotional development levels. Analyses were conducted in R using the MASS package. Results: Ordinal regression analyses revealed significant associations between mental disorder diagnoses, ID severity and emotional development levels with self-injurious, stereotyped and aggressive behaviours. ID severity and emotional development levels were the strongest predictors, whereas the effect of mental disorder diagnoses was more limited but remained significant in interaction models, particularly for self-injurious and aggressive behaviours. Conclusions: These findings highlight the complex interplay between emotional development, ID severity, mental disorders and challenging behaviours. A clinical perspective will also be considered, as emotional development plays a crucial role in ensuring that these results guide the adaptation of support strategies in practice.

Title: Deinstitutionalization in the Care of Persons With Intellectual Disabilities and Psychiatric and/or Behavioural Problems: Collaboration Between Residential and Mobile Care
Abstract Note: Background: De-institutionalization within the care of persons with intellectual disabilities and additional psychiatric and/or behavioural problems requires a systematic and personalized approach. The transition from institutional to community-based care implies a close collaboration between residential facilities and mobile teams, where continuity and tailored support are central. This presentation highlights the implementation of an integrated treatment pathway achieved through structured collaboration between the two care structures. The goal is to ensure continuity of care beyond residential admission, emphasizing individualized pre-and post-admission processes. Methods: An interdisciplinary approach is applied, involving structured consultations and joint decision-making. A dynamic treatment plan is developed, tailored to the client's specific needs, ensuring seamless transitions between care settings. Results: Using a real-life case study, it is demonstrated that this integrated approach optimizes transitions and minimizes the risk of relapse. Early intervention and proactive support promote stability in the home situation and improve the client's quality of life. Conclusions: Efficient collaboration between residential and mobile services contributes to a reduction in long-term residential admissions and enhances the effectiveness of care delivery.

Title: The Impact of the Emotional Development Level in Neuropsychiatric Disorders and Problem Behaviour in People With Intellectual Disability: A Study in a Spanish Context
Abstract Note: Background: People with ID present often a disparity between emotional and cognitive competencies, playing a possible role in the onset of some psychiatric disorders and problem behaviour. Methods: We carried out an observational and cross-sectional study from 192 adults with ID and psychiatric disorders. Results: We found a possible relationship between emotional development level and intellectual disability degree, as well as with problem behaviour severity and with some kind of neuropsychiatric and neurodevelopmental disorders. Conclusions: The emotional development level is a key factor in the problem behaviour severity and in the onset of some psychiatric disorders in people with ID.

Title: Presentation of Adults With Intellectual Disability and Neurodevelopmental Conditions Across Forensic Services and Criminal Justice Pathways
Abstract Note: Background: The study of offenders with intellectual disability including those with neurodevelopmental conditions has grown over the past 30 years with an increase understanding of the complexity of their presentation across forensic services and the criminal justice system. Methods: Papers were selected to provide a European perspective on how different countries approach working with adults with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental conditions whose behaviour reaches the threshold for criminal justice by summarizing key research in this area including describing current practice with a focus on the Nordic countries of Norway and Denmark and a review of the evidence across Europe of those within the prison systems. The final paper provides a more detailed picture of young adults with neurodevelopmental conditions in contact with the court system in London, England. Results: There is variation in approaches across countries to this vulnerable group of offenders with high rates of co-occurring conditions and vulnerabilities such as risk for self-harm behaviour. Conclusions: Forensic and Criminal Justice Services across Europe need to be aware of vulnerabilities of this group of offenders and provide appropriate support with a tailored approach to assessment and interventions.

Title: Solving Complexity by Collaboration: Optimizing Mental Health Care in Smith- Magenis Syndrome
Abstract Note: Background: The Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMs) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder caused by a 17p11.2 deletion or a pathogenic variant of the RAI1 gene, which lies within the 17p11.2 region. SMs is associated with congenital and later-onset health issues and an array of neuropsychiatric disorders, such as intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit (hyperactivity) disorder (ad(H)D), self-injurious behaviours (SIB), aggressive behaviours, and severe sleep-wake disorders. These complex behaviours typically pose a challenge for families and clinicians. Methods: In this presentation, a psychiatrist and ID physician with a longstanding professional collaboration will present results of joint research including data from a clinical cohort of children and adults with SMs and a systematic review exploring psychiatric disorders in adults with SMs. In addition, the presenters will discuss key factors for successful clinical collaboration. Results: Findings of the systematic review and clinical experience indicate that the vast majority of children and adults with SMs present with psychiatric manifestations, with psychiatric disorders that are common in childhood persisting into adulthood. However, systematic studies using standardized diagnostic criteria are basically non-existing, and current knowledge is based on a limited number of patients. Clinical experiences indicate that a stepwise and integrative approach offers the best chance of successful treatment. Conclusions: SMs is associated with high prevalence of psychiatric disorders, but research is needed to further characterize the psychiatric phenotype. Multidisciplinary collaboration between clinicians is crucial to facilitate optimization of management strategies in children and adults with SMs. There is a need for evidence-based clinical guidelines for management of psychiatric disorders in SMs.

Title: Psychometric Properties of the Social Information Processing Test for Adults With Mild ID
Abstract Note: Background: Adults with ID show more externalizing behaviour compared to adults without ID. Dysfunctional social cognition is one of the underlying factors of externalizing behaviour. Dysfunctional social cognition can be described in terms of deviances in Social Information Processing (SIP). An instrument that assesses all separate SIP steps is the Social Information Processing Test (SIVT) developed for children and adolescents. The child and adolescent version of the SIVT showed adequate or good internal consistency, interrater reliability, content validity and criterium validity. Based on the experiences in daily practice with these versions, and the link between disturbances in SIP and externalizing behaviour in adults with mild ID, a need for an adult version was stated, with its own realistic situations and interpretations. Therefore, the Social Information Processing Test for adults (SIVT-V) was developed, and its psychometric properties were assessed. Methods: Adults with mild ID and adults from the general population between 18 and 60 years were included. With all these adults the SIVT-V was administered, an interactive test with six videos in which realistic problematic social situations is shown and a structured interview is held about the SIP skills. Previous to each video, they were asked to imagine that the participant was the victim in the specific situation. There was a version for young adults aged 18-30 years and a version for adults aged 31-60 years, with identical situations, but different actors. For (young) adults with mild ID, the subscale externalizing behaviour of the ASR was also assessed for the level of behaviour problems and the screeners SCIL and SCAF to validate for mild ID. Different forms of validity were assessed, and group differences between (young) adults with and without ID for different SIP steps were investigated. Results: At the congress, results of the different forms of validity, internal consistency and group differences will be presented. Conclusions: At the congress, the results will be discussed, including its implications for practice, policy and further research.

Title: A scoping review investigating the perspectives of people with mild to moderate intellectual disabilities on experiences of cyberbullying victimisation and its subtypes
Abstract Note: This scoping review examines cyberbullying victimisation in people with mild to moderate intellectual disabilities, focusing on specific types of cyberbullying behaviours, such as flaming, harassment, and stalking. A five-stage review of empirical research was conducted using 15 electronic databases, covering publications from October 1969 to January 2024. Twelve studies were selected, reporting cyberbullying victimisation rates ranging from 5% to 64%. Harassment was the most common behaviour experienced. However, flaming, cyber-stalking, griefing, and shaming have not been thoroughly investigated. The impact and coping strategies, including support mechanisms, also lack research. Further investigation is needed to understand the various types of cyberbullying experienced by people with intellectual disabilities and to develop coping and resilience strategies. Recommendations for future research and practice are provided.

Title: Close Relationships Despite the Challenges: Sibling Relationships and Autism
Abstract Note: This study explores the experiences of siblings of autistic adolescents within families. Without the novel insights generated from engaging with siblings of autistic adolescents within a qualitative framework, it can be challenging to develop strategies for practicing effectively with this group or structuring interventions with these families. Using a social constructivist approach and qualitative participatory methodology, the exploratory study was conducted using in-depth interviews with ten non-autistic siblings, analyzed via a thematic analysis method. The results reveal a common feeling of uncertainty and apprehension in the relationships, leading siblings to physical and emotional detachment from their autistic brothers or sisters. The research emphasizes the caregiving roles predominantly taken up by sisters, especially when the autistic sibling is a brother with intellectual disability. These roles exert substantial demands, with unclear boundaries suggesting potential role confusion. The findings have important implications for family practice, necessitating the need to address role conflict and promote role clarity. They also underscore the gendered nature of caregiving, advocating for support to sister-siblings in these roles. This study revealed the complexities of sibling relationships in families with a member who is an autistic adolescent sibling. The study suggests interventions that promote open family dialogues for a balanced approach to family roles, providing valuable guidance to practitioners to enhance siblings and family well-being.

Title: Factors affecting the feelings of safety among individuals with mild intellectual disabilities and severe challenging behaviour in residential care: A qualitative study of professional and service users’ perspectives
Abstract Note: This qualitative study focuses on what feeling safe means for people with mild intellectual disabilities and severe challenging behaviour, and which factors affect their sense of safety. Thematic analysis was used to analyse data collected during (1) ethnographic longitudinal research and (2) interviews and focus groups among professionals and service users. Feelings of safety were related to three main themes: (1) a physical environment that reduces risks and temptations; (2) a reliable, predictable, and supportive environment; and (3) an accepting environment that enables service users to establish a normal life. An analysis of which factors affect service users’ sense of safety identified 20 themes (e.g. team climate) and 34 subthemes (e.g. interactions with other service users). Many of these factors were interconnected. Future research should explore what residential service organisations for people with intellectual disabilities and external actors (e.g. the police) can do to promote service users’ feelings of safety.

Title: Mental and Behavioral Health, and Crisis Services for People with Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities in Medicaid Home- and Community-Based Services
Abstract Note: People with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) often have higher rates of comorbid mental health conditions compared to the general population. Yet, many people with IDD also have unmet needs for mental and behavioral health services. The aim of this study was to examine how states provided mental and behavior health, and crisis services to people with IDD in their Home- and Community-Based Services (HCBS) programs, the largest funding mechanism for Long-Term Services and Supports (LTSS) for people with IDD in the United States. We analyzed fiscal year (2021) Medicaid HCBS waivers for people with IDD from across the United States to examine if and how they provided mental and behavior health, and crisis services. States projected spending $968.9 million for mental and behavior health, and crisis services for 190,299 people with IDD. Applied behavior analysis services were provided at greater rates than positive behavior supports and other forms of behavior interventions. While most states provided mental and behavior health, and crisis services in their waivers, there were vast inconsistencies in how they did so, across states, waivers, and services. HCBS are a crucial safety net to ensure people with IDD, especially those who also have mental health disabilities, can live and thrive in their communities.

Title: Parents' and Healthcare Professionals' Experiences in Interprofessional Collaboration in Rare Genetic Intellectual Disability Syndrome: A Qualitative Study Into Barriers and Facilitators
Abstract Note: Background: People with rare genetic intellectual disability syndromes (RGIDS) have physical and mental health related problems, with a high risk for challenging behaviour (e.g., aggression, self-injury). They rely on integrated and specialized expertise of numerous healthcare professionals across medical care, intellectual disability (ID) care, mental care and social care. Additionally, parents are often experts in their child's genetic syndrome, health, and behaviour and play a key role in interacting with and connecting professionals involved in their child's care. However, interprofessional collaboration with parents and healthcare professionals is challenging. In daily practice, professionals often work in silos, with limited communication and lack of coordination in care. While medical issues and genetic diagnosis receive primary attention, parents frequently experience a gap in behavioural care. Consequently, parents often find themselves taking on a professional role, which may not always be within their capabilities, underscoring the need for improved interprofessional collaboration. This study explored the barriers and facilitators experienced by parents and healthcare professionals in interprofessional collaboration. Methods: A qualitative approach was used, interviewing parents and healthcare professionals of people with RGIDS and challenging behaviour. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using thematic analyses. Data was collected until sufficiency was reached. Results: The results will outline the barriers and facilitators experienced by parents and healthcare professionals in interprofessional collaboration. As the interviews are currently being conducted and require analysis, the findings are expected to be presented in September 2025. Conclusion: By understanding the barriers and facilitators in interprofessional collaboration (with parents in an expert role), we expect to identify areas for improvement and unravel professional competences to enhance interprofessional collaboration and address what is needed to adequately service and treat families of RGIDS people. This study is designed to hopefully unburden parents, allowing them to collaborate more as experts in their child's care.

Title: An Investigation of Autonomic Function in SYNGAP1-Related Intellectual Disability
Abstract Note: Background: Dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system may play a role in the presence of behaviours that challenge. This relationship is particularly relevant in SYNGAP1-related intellectual disability (ID), a non-inherited ID in which behaviours such as physical aggression and self-injury are commonly reported. Methods: To investigate autonomic function in SYNGAP1, we recruited 21 individuals with SYNGAP1 and 15 typically developing controls (TDC) to measure autonomic function via heart rate variability (HRV) analysis. An electrocardiogram (ECG) recording was collected while participants watched a 20-minute film-based paradigm with baseline, calming and arousing blocks. Analysis of the ECG was conducted using HeartPy, where time-domain and frequency-domain HRV metrics were calculated for each block. Aligned rank transformation ANOVAs were conducted, where HRV metrics were compared by group (SYNGAP1 vs. TDC). Results: Between group differences were apparent across all three conditions when examining beats per minute (BPM) (F(1, 31) = 15.40, p < 0.001), as well as traditional HRV metrics, such as time domain (pNN50: F(1, 31) = 7.04, p = 0.01)) and frequency domain (high-frequency: F(1, 31) = 5.79, p = 0.02)) measures. BPM was higher in the SYNGAP1 group when compared with TDC, while the pNN50 and high-frequency measures, which are both influenced by parasympathetic tone, were lower in the SYNGAP1 group compared with TDC. Additional time-and frequency-domain measures were assessed (i.e., RMSSD, SDNN, very-low-frequency and low-frequency), in which differences between groups approached significance in some metrics (RMSSD, very-low-frequency) and were not different between groups in other measures (SDNN, low-frequency). Between condition differences were observed in certain metrics, including RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50 and high-frequency; all measures were higher during the calming condition in both groups. There were no significant group by condition interactions. Conclusions: These results demonstrate a decrease in parasympathetic tone in individuals with SYNGAP1-related ID compared with TDC; this may contribute to increased levels of distress.

Title: Brief Report: Evaluating the Impact of Behavioural Concerns in Individuals With Intellectual or Developmental Disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: Behavioural concerns, such as aggression and self-injury, are common among youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities. Additional research is needed to further explore the specific ways in which these types of behaviour impact individuals and their families. Methods: Caregivers seeking treatment for their child's behavioural concerns completed an interview regarding the negative impact of their child's behaviour related to (a) physical harm to self or others, (b) property damage, (c) structural modifications, (d) situational avoidance and (e) reactive measures. We reviewed outcomes of these interviews to report on the prevalence of various negative impacts in this clinical sample. Results: Most caregivers reported at least some physical harm (72.99%), property damage (63.99%) and preventative measures such as avoiding removing preferred items or activities (72.35%). Some caregivers endorsed severe negative impacts, such as the need for emergency services (10.61%) or residential placements (5.14%). Conclusions: Caregivers in this clinical sample consistently endorsed negative impacts resulting from behavioural concerns. This information is crucial in advocating for additional services for this high-need population, and the interview used to gather this information may be a helpful tool to guide future research and clinical work.

Title: The Effect of SPECTROM Training on Support Staff Knowledge of Psychotropic Medicine and Attitude Towards Behaviours That Challenge in Adults With Intellectual Disabilities to Help Implement the STOMP Initiative
Abstract Note: Background: Overmedication of adults with intellectual (learning) disabilities, particularly the off-licence use of psychotropic medicines for behaviours that challenge in the absence of a psychiatric disorder, is a major public health concern and an example of health inequalities. In the United Kingdom, we coproduced online training resources backed up by face-to-face training for support staff (direct care workers) called SPECTROM involving all stakeholders, including adults with intellectual disabilities and their families, to help reduce the overmedication and implement NHS England's STOMP initiative. Method: In a feasibility cluster randomised controlled trial, we trained service managers and support staff using two core modules of SPECTROM, namely, (a) Medicine/STOMP and (b) Alternatives to Medicine (ATM) using an online platform. These two core modules introduced 12 other modules and other online resources. We assessed trainees' knowledge of psychotropic medicines using the Psychotropic Knowledge Questionnaire-Revised (PKQ-R) and their attitude to behaviours that challenge using the Management of Aggression and Violence Attitude Scale-Revised-Intellectual Disabilities (MAVAS-R-ID) using a pre–post training design. Results: The research team delivered SPECTROM training to 18 service managers and 122 support staff. Of the 140 trainees, 126 completed PKQ-R at baseline before and within 4 weeks after the training. There was a post-training improvement in PKQ-R scores in 42 of the 43 questions (97.7%), 22 of which were statistically significant differences (p < 0.001). The MAVAS-R-ID was completed at baseline and within 4 weeks of training by 125 trainees. The MAVAS-R-ID total score showed statistically significant post-training improvements (p < 0.01). Individual domain score analysis showed a statistically significant improvement in one of the five domains related to attitude regarding the use of medicine for behaviours that challenge. Conclusions: The SPECTROM training seems to improve staff knowledge of psychotropic medicine, at least in the short-term, and attitude towards behaviours that challenge, particularly concerning the use of psychotropic medicine.

Title: A systematic review of studies on the association between physiological parameters and self-harm
Abstract Note: Background: Self-harm is common in people with intellectual disabilities and is associated with multiple adverse consequences for the client engaging in self-harm, other clients and caregivers. Self-harm is related to emotional dysregulation according to both observational and self-report data. Measures of the autonomic nervous system might provide additional insight in this relationship. Methods: The current systematic review systematically summarized a broad spectrum of studies on the association between self-harm and physiological parameters. The search identified 2400 articles, 46 were included. Results: In most studies, which compared electrodermal activity and heart rate in people with and without self-harm, no clear indications for a relation between physiology and self-harm was found. Studies on heart rate variability showed indications for lower heart rate variability during recovery, which could imply emotion dysregulation, findings which were supported by results from imagery studies (heart rate and skin conductance). No consistent findings were found when self-harm was studied before, during or after actual occurrences of self-harm, although this was examined by very few studies. Conclusions: Although wearable technology has improved, the majority of studies to date are lab-studies. Future research should focus on measuring physiology in daily life before, during and after self-harm, in people with intellectual disabilities, study different types and functions of self-harm separately, and test multimodal prediction models. This knowledge could improve the understanding, prevention and assessment of this debilitating behaviour.

Title: Type, content, and triggers for self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in autistic youth and their disclosure to caregivers
Abstract Note: Rates of self-injurious thoughts and behaviors are elevated among autistic youth, yet research is limited to caregiver report or single-item questionnaires. Investigation of specific suicidal thoughts, triggers, and disclosure is needed to improve risk assessment and interventions. The current study characterized self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in a sample of autistic youth without intellectual disability presenting for outpatient psychological services. The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale and qualitative follow-up questions were administered to 103 autistic youth (10–17 years of age). Most autistic youth (n = 86; 83.5%) reported lifetime suicidal thoughts. Suicide thought content most commonly included abstract thoughts of dying/suicide (n = 20; 23.3%) and death by cutting (n = 13; 15.1%). Half of youth experiencing suicidal thoughts (n = 43; 50.0%) denied disclosure to their caregiver. Nearly one in four youth attempted suicide (n = 25; 24.3%), and some youth (n = 16; 15.5%) sought help from caregivers to prevent an attempt. Sadness/depression and bullying/teasing were the most commonly reported triggers of suicidal behaviors. Among autistic youth with lifetime nonsuicidal self-injury (n = 52; 50.5%), head hitting (n = 28; 45.2%) and cutting (n = 20; 32.3%) were the most reported types. Findings underscore the importance of targeted prevention and intervention to address self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in autistic youth and continued research to understand barriers and modifiable factors to facilitate self-injurious thoughts and behaviors disclosure. Lay abstract: Self-injurious thoughts and behaviors are high among autistic youth, yet research most often relies on caregiver reports and does not include youth perspectives. Relatedly, specific characteristics of self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (e.g. type of behavior, thought content, triggers), and choices to share these thoughts and behaviors with caregivers/parents (or not), have not been studied in autistic youth. With limited information on self-injurious thoughts and behaviors in autistic youth, clinicians and families supporting autistic youth in crisis continue to experience major challenges to best assess and support youth. Therefore, to begin to understand youth perspectives of self-injurious thoughts and behaviors, we administered a self-injurious thoughts and behaviors clinical interview (Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale; C-SSRS) to 103 autistic youth without intellectual disability (10–17 years of age) at a clinic for outpatient mental health services. We added follow-up questions to the interview about suicide to better understand what youth think about when it comes to suicide, what triggers them to feel suicidal, and whether they let their caregiver know about what they are thinking and feeling. Results show that most autistic youth reported suicidal thoughts at some point in their life (n = 86; 83.5%), with thoughts of dying/suicide (n = 20; 23.3%) and death by cutting (n = 13; 15.1%) as common thought content. Half of youth experiencing suicidal thoughts (n = 43; 50.0%) did not share this with their caregiver. Nearly one in four youth had attempted suicide at some point in their life (n = 25; 24.3%), while some youth (n = 16; 15.5%) sought help from caregivers to prevent an attempt. Sadness/depression and bullying/teasing were the most common triggers of suicidal behaviors, while anger/frustration was the leading trigger for nonsuicidal self-injury. Findings can be used to improve current assessment tools and prevention approaches for autistic youth to create better support for autistic youth in crisis.

Title: Psychosocial factors associated with the trajectories of interparental conflict for Australian fathers of autistic children: A longitudinal study across 10 years of child development
Abstract Note: Limited research exists on fathers’ experiences of interparental conflict (IPC) in families with autistic children. We aimed to identify: (1) the extent to which these fathers report IPC across 10 years of child development (4–14 years) and how this compares to fathers of non-autistic children; (2) distinct trajectories of IPC for fathers of autistic children and (3) factors associated with trajectories of IPC among fathers of autistic children. This is a retrospective study using a national dataset. Participants were 281 fathers of autistic children and 7046 fathers of non-autistic children. Although small effect sizes, fathers of autistic children, on average, reported significantly higher IPC when their child was 4–5, 6–7, 8–9 and 10–12 years of age, compared to fathers of non-autistic children. For fathers of autistic children, longitudinal latent class analysis revealed three profiles reflecting ‘low and stable’, ‘moderate and stable’ and ‘persistently elevated’ levels of IPC over time. Regression analysis revealed a range of predictors (e.g. co-parenting support, father age) for fathers of autistic children experiencing ‘moderate and stable’ and ‘persistently elevated’ IPC as compared to fathers who experienced low levels of IPC. There is a significant portion of fathers of autistic children who experience ongoing and heightened IPC, highlighting the need for targeted support. Lay Abstract: Not much is known about how fathers experience conflict with their partners (either verbal or physical) while raising an autistic child. This study focused on understanding these experiences over 10 years, following children from the age of 4 to 14 years. The study had two main goals: (1) to track how fathers experience conflict with their partners over this time and identify different patterns to these experiences; and (2) to find psychosocial factors in early childhood that might impact these patterns. The study included 281 fathers of autistic children and 7046 fathers of non-autistic children who took part in ‘Growing Up in Australia: Longitudinal Study of Australian Children’. Using a statistical method to group fathers based on the partner conflict they reported over the 10 years, results showed that there were three groups: (1) ‘low and stable’, (2) ‘moderate and stable’ and (3) ‘persistently elevated’ experiences of partner conflict. Additional analysis showed that fathers’ confidence in their parenting, perceived support from their partners and concerns about their child’s language skills were associated with ongoing moderate levels of partner conflict. On the other hand, fathers who were older, had lower perceived support from their partners, partners experiencing psychological distress and higher parent-reported child social functioning were more likely to experience consistently high levels of conflict over time. In our study, we described different levels of conflict with their partners reported by fathers of autistic children. We also identified some of the factors that were associated with different levels of conflict. These might be used to inform interventions to reduce parental conflict in the future.

Title: Prospective Characterisation of Age-Related Changes in Self-Injurious Behaviour in a Sample of Children With Global Developmental Delay Aged 2–12 Years
Abstract Note: Background: Self-injurious behaviour (SIB) is a common problem among individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDDs) with important impacts on quality of life. Although some evidence suggests that SIB may increase with age, perhaps in a curvilinear pattern, this is primarily based on cross-sectional studies. Therefore, the purpose of the current study was to conduct a prospective, longitudinal analysis of age-related changes in a high-risk cohort of children with developmental disabilities/delays. Methods: A total of 110 participants, between 2 and 12 years of age at enrolment (70% male), were followed for between 2 and 4 years. Caregivers completed the RBS-EC SIB subscale annually, for a total of 317 assessments. The SIB total score, SIB interference ratings and endorsement of specific topographies were selected as dependent measures. Generalised linear models evaluating linear, quadratic and cubic age-related changes and differences by intellectual disability (ID) status (no or mild ID vs. moderate to profound ID) were created for each outcome. Results: For SIB total scores, the model suggested complex developmental patterns that varied by degree of ID. For SIB interference ratings, the model suggested that individuals with moderate to profound ID showed relatively high and stable levels of SIB interference across ages, whereas individuals with no or mild ID showed an increasing trend with age. Patterns varied across the specific SIB topographies. Discussion: The results suggest that age-related changes in SIB are complex and may vary across topographies. Overall, the results are concerning in that they indicate a potentially increasing trend in frequency of SIB and its impact on daily activities as individuals approach adolescence, indicating the need for further longitudinal work across the lifespan.

Title: Predictive Validity of the Brøset Violence Checklist in a Secured Institution for Offenders With Intellectual Disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: The integration of systematic risk assessments into care settings for offenders with intellectual disabilities (IDs) is a growing priority, yet evidence on the validity of existing tools in this population remains limited. The Brøset Violence Checklist (BVC) is widely used to assess short-term violence risk, but its predictive accuracy in individuals with IDs remains uncertain. This study investigates the predictive validity of the BVC in a specialized institutional context for offenders with IDs, focusing on its performance across different shifts and demographic subgroups. Method: A retrospective observational design was used to analyse 153 262 BVC assessments and 1325 documented severe violent incidents over 2.5 years in a secured Danish institution for offenders with IDs. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were calculated across different BVC thresholds. Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) were applied to assess the influence of sex and time of day on predictive performance. Results: The BVC demonstrated high specificity and NPV across all shifts, confirming its utility in identifying low-risk scenarios. However, sensitivity and PPV were limited, particularly during night shifts and at higher score thresholds. Predictive accuracy was highest during evening shifts, aligning with periods of increased staff–resident interactions. GLMM analyses indicated that the relationship between BVC scores and violence risk was moderated by sex and time of day, with female residents and low-activity periods presenting unique challenges to prediction. Conclusions: The findings underscore the need for population-specific adaptations to the BVC, particularly to address contextual and demographic factors influencing aggression in ID populations. Recommendations include supplemental assessment strategies for low-activity shifts, sex-specific behavioural indicators and the development of tailored tools for ID care settings. This study advances the understanding of violence risk dynamics in ID populations and informs interventions to enhance safety for residents and staff.

Title: Sharing the stage: Inclusion theater programming, social participation, and quality of life
Abstract Note: Background: Social participation is a crucial Quality of Life (QoL) factor. Inclusion theater programming allows rehabilitation providers to collaborate with arts professionals to provide rich, authentic, inclusive therapeutic experiences for individuals with communication disorders secondary to intellectual and developmental disabilities and neurodivergence. Methods: Qualitative thematic analysis was used to examine semi-structured interviews with five parents of children with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) or neurodivergence regarding their child's participation in an inclusion theater program. Results: Parents described a typical social landscape that discourages social participation for neurodivergent children and children and adolescents with IDD. They appreciated the structure of this inclusion theater program, which they contrasted with their child's everyday reality. They described that both program design and personnel supported individualized learning. Perceived benefits included development of friendships and a sense of belonging within a community, along with encouraging demonstrations of confidence and self-advocacy. While this opportunity was held up to contrast their everyday social reality of exclusion and bullying, parents found this singular annual program insufficient. They pledged to advocate for better community education to expand inclusion opportunities. Discussion: Social participation, a key QoL element, was observed by parents of children engaged in this inclusion theater program and credited for perceived positive benefits. Parents believed that the structure of the program promoted learning and skill growth, increases in personal factors such as confidence and self-advocacy, along with development of community, and a sense of responsibility that empowered the children. Success experienced in such programming can lead parents and children to try more mainstream opportunities.
