Title: The experiences of teachers of children with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) in inclusive schools in Accra, Ghana
Abstract Note: Introduction: Inclusive education is the best form of education for all children. However, children with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) are often educated in segregated settings or institutionalized, in developing contexts such as Ghana. An understanding of teachers' experiences with children with IDD in inclusion may inform strategies for more effective inclusive systems for children with IDD. Methods: A qualitative descriptive approach was adopted that involved semi-structured interviews with 15 regular and two special educators in inclusive schools in Accra, Ghana. Results: Teachers have positive and negative experiences regarding inclusion. Teachers' negative experiences include challenges with support services for children with problem behaviours and parents of children with IDD. Teacher's main positive experience is the satisfaction felt when children with IDD show progress in inclusion. Teachers shared their perspectives of strategies that might facilitate the inclusion of children with IDD in Ghana in the future. Implications: Identifying and addressing factors accounting for teacher negative experiences while supporting and promoting positive experiences may help identify specific and appropriate strategies that are tailored to the unique characteristics of children with IDD. This may facilitate inclusive environments and create more conducive spaces for the accommodation of diversity and improvement outcomes for children with IDD in Ghana and across the globe.

Title: Peer support for mothers with intellectual disability facing adversity
Abstract Note: Introduction: Peer support can help vulnerable and isolated families engage with social services and navigate child protection systems. Parents with intellectual disability are highly disadvantaged and at risk of child removal but little is known about their experience of peer support. An inclusive study was undertaken to address the gap. Methods: Researchers interviewed twenty-six parents with intellectual disability. Inductive content analysis was used to identify themes. One theme revealed the influence of peer support to cope with life challenges. Ten participating mothers had experienced statutory child removal and/or domestic and family violence. Results: Mothers described feelings of loss, grief, anger, and betrayal. Fragile family networks and fear of child removal created mistrust of professionals. Peers were a trusted source of advice and support to cope with emotional pain. Participants who attended a support group described the importance of respect, equality and mutuality from peers. Implications: Peers are a valued and trusted source of support for mothers with intellectual disability. These highly vulnerable women often have limited informal support and view professionals with suspicion. Peer-based advocacy models for parents in the child protection system must take steps to become disability inclusive. Peers need training to support mothers facing significant grief and trauma.

Title: Measuring symbolic functioning and visuo-motor skills for appropriate approaches to teenagers with low verbal communication and aggressive behaviors
Abstract Note: Introduction: A person's cognition affects his or her social behaviors. A system of practical evaluation of cognition and social behaviours had not been established in this setting, in Japan. Methods: The author assessed cognitive functions of two teenagers with intellectual disability who showed strongly aggressive behaviors, employing an evaluation method measuring symbolic functioning and visuo-motor skills. Case A showed hyper-activity and touching behaviors toward others, that included picking up dust from their clothes. Case B showed sudden, swift grasping actions at others' arms as an expression of his anger. Both scored extremely high in the Aberrant Behavior Checklist-Community Japanese version (ABC-J). School teachers and welfare practitioners in the learners' after-school day service, collaborated in improving treatments for the teenagers and in rewriting their individual plans according to the evaluation results. Results: The learners showed clearly different levels of symbolic functioning and qualitative differences between language comprehension skills and visual perception skills respectively, although they were both diagnosed as individuals with severe intellectual disability. The appropriate management which reduced such behaviors was different depending on each learner's cognitive level. Implications: Individuals with severe intellectual disability have diverse presentation. Appropriate approaches were guided from cognitive assessments and individualization based on different cognitive status by all multidisciplinary staff was beneficial.

Title: Behavioural profile of anxiety in autistic individuals with few or no words and individuals with genetic syndromes associated with intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are at increased risk of anxiety (estimated prevalence of 40%). This study examined parent reported behavioural markers of anxiety in autistic individuals and individuals with genetic syndromes associated with ASD who speak few or no words. Methods: A semi-structured interview was completed with parents/ carers, along with the Social Communication Questionnaire, the Wessex Questionnaire and the Anxiety, Depression and Mood Scale (ADAMS). Results: To date, 25 interviews have been completed. The behavioural markers of anxiety most frequently endorsed by parents were increased vocalisation (n = 18) and self-injury (n = 13). Frequently endorsed triggers of anxiety were routine changes (n = 17) and sensory overload (n = 15). In the interview, anxiety severity and the total number of anxiety triggers correlated with the ADAMS general anxiety subscale (rs = .434, p < 0.05; rs = .462, p < 0.05 respectively). Autistic individuals scored higher on the general anxiety subscale of the ADAMS and had a higher number of triggers compared to individuals with genetic syndromes (U = 14.5, p < 0.05; U = 19.5, p < 0.05 respectively). Implications: These data will be used to inform the development of a clinical assessment tool for anxiety for autistic individuals with ID to be utilised within healthcare services.

Title: Sibling experiences in families of individuals with williams syndrome
Abstract Note: Introduction: Although individuals with Williams syndrome (WS) are known to be at heightened risk for anxiety disorders and social victimization, families of these individuals frequently report positive effects of having a child with WS. However, few studies have been conducted examining outcomes for siblings of this population. Methods: We used an online survey to collect data from 20 siblings of individuals with Williams syndrome on stress, the sibling relationship, and behavior problems. These data were compared to existing results from siblings of individuals with autism spectrum disorder and Down syndrome. Results: Siblings reported that parents showed preferential treatment to the child with WS, but did not report any significant unbalance in the sibling relationship. Neither behavior problems among the individual with WS nor the sibling relationship correlated with sibling self-reported stress. Additionally, WS-Sibs reported significantly less overall stress than siblings of individuals with autism, even when controlling for sibling age and brother/sister behavior problems (B = -1.68, p<.001). Implications: These results can help families and service providers better service families with WS and other intellectual disabilities by identifying factors that are important to siblings. Additionally, further studying the low levels among WS-Sibs can help researchers identify protective factors that can then be used to support families of individuals with other types of disability.

Title: The association of life events and mental ill health in older adults with intellectual disability: Results of the wave 3 intellectual disability supplement to the irish longitudinal study on ageing (IDS-TILDA)
Abstract Note: Introduction: Exposures to life events are associated with emotional, psychological and behavioural problems in those with intellectual disability (ID). Older adults with ID may experience different life events given differences in living circumstances, cognitive decline and less autonomy. Methods: The study was part of “The Intellectual Disability Supplement to the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing” (IDS-TILDA). The frequency of life events was assessed using a 20-item checklist and the level of stress experienced using a three-point Likert scale. The associations of life events with factors associated with mental ill health were measured using self-report and proxy completed questionnaires. Results: For the study population, 88.1% had been exposed to at least one life event in the preceding 12 months. Frequency and burden of life events were significantly higher in individuals with any current psychiatric condition, increased depressive and anxiety symptoms, challenging behaviour and reported poorer self-rated mental and physical health. More life events were significantly associated with new psychiatric diagnoses, initiation and increased dosage of mood stabilising, hypnotic and sedative medications. Implications: Life events are significantly associated with mental ill health in the older ID population. Service providers must focus on limiting the exposure to these events and and in situations where they cannot be avoided, should support and manage individuals compassionately and effectively, prioritising their mental and physical well-being.

Title: Profiles of people with intellectual disabilities and criminal justice involvement in community mental health services
Abstract Note: Introduction: This study estimated the prevalence of intellectual disabilities (ID) among adults with and without criminal justice (CJ) involvement enrolled in community mental health and addictions (MH&A) services in Ontario, Canada. This study described the sociodemographic characteristics, clinical characteristics, and use of health care services for persons with CJ involvement and ID relative to people with CJ involvement only. Methods: This cross-sectional study involved 41,367 adults aged 18- 64 in community MH&A programs in Ontario, Canada from 2011 to 2016 who had completed a needs assessment data. Results: Prevalence of ID was not different for people with CJ involvement (7.9%) versus people with no CJ involvement who have ID (8.1%). Relative to people with CJ involvement, people with ID and CJ involvement were more likely to have issues with safety to others, issues with self-harm, and met or unmet functional needs. They were also less likely to have a psychiatrist, but had little difference in their acute care utilisation patterns. Implications: In community MH&A services, the proportion of individuals with CJ involvement who had DD was similar to the proportion of others with no CJ involvement. More attention is needed to issues of safety to others and to self among this group. Efforts to support people with ID prior to CJ involvement would also be advantageous.

Title: Intervention moment: Developing family resources to cope with challenging behavior
Abstract Note: Introduction: Parents of children with intellectual disabilities have reported a need for guidance to cope with children's challenging behavior. Existing family school models as such are not suitable for families with special needs. The aim of this research, conducted in Finland, is to develop a model to reverse negative parent-child interaction by increasing positive interaction and parents' resources. The theoretical background to the study is systems theory (Fogel 1993), mentalization theory (Fonagy 2008) and attachment theory (Bowlby 1969). Methods: The resource-driven peer group model was developed as an action study. Data was collected when six family groups met every second week for a total of 8 times. Studies have shown that long-term 8- 20 week programs are effective in reducing behavioral problems in children. The functionality of the model was examined by participating in the group sessions by observing. A total of 36 families participated in the development afer which the model was evaluated. Parents were interviewed before and after participating in the group. Results: According to findings, parents initially saw the challenging behavior as associated with the child's internal deficiencies in emotional and social skills, but did not see the interaction built as bidirectionally. After group sessions parents reported having more resources to support their children, and the children having fewer behavioral challenges. Implications: The model was effective in increasing parents' resources to addressing negative parent-child interactions.

Title: A study on research trends of peer mediated interventions for students with severe intellectual disabilities
Abstract Note: Introduction: Peers are the most useful natural resource within general classes that can support the various educational demands of students with severe intellectual disabilities. This study aims to investigate research trends regarding peer mediated interventions for the students. Methods: A total of 17 articles regarding peer mediated interventions published from 1990 to 2019 were analysed in detail using the following factors: research participants and settings, experimental design, intervener (peer selection criteria, training contents and strategies, training termination criteria), independent, and dependent variables. Results: The findings showed that the studies mostly focused on elementary school students and general classroom settings. About the design of experiments, the most of studies applied multiple baseline design. The analysis of intervener showed four types of criteria used in peer selection. Peer training contents included teaching and applying intervention strategies, methods to communicate and feedback to their partners. Peer training strategies used modeling, role playing and error correction feedback, and the printed materials. Peer training was terminated when peers met 80% of the performance expected. Positive results have been reported in terms of the access to the general education curriculum (participating behaviours, academic achievement), functional skills, social interaction and skills, and problem behaviours. Implications: Based on the results, practical implications and directions for future research are provided to promote inclusive education for students with severe intellectual disabilities by peer mediated interventions.

Title: A self-determination theory perspective: Results of a longitudinal study into the need satisfaction and well-being of people with mild to borderline intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Self-determination is an essential dimension of quality of life. Self-determination theory (SDT) relates three basic psychological needs to self-determination: autonomy, relatedness, and competence. It has been argued that these needs are universally important. However, research on these needs in people with intellectual disability (ID) is scarce. Recently, we examined the relationship between the psychological needs and well-being/ill-being in 186 people with mild to borderline ID. In this study, we invited participants of our previous study to participate in this longitudinal study in which we revisited them 4.5 years after their first partaking. Methods: Hundred-and-fifteen participants (61.8%) provided informed consent to participate in this longitudinal study. Participants completed various measurements on psychological needs (Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale - Intellectual Disability), autonomy support (Healthcare Climate Questionnaire), motivation (the Self-Regulation Questionnaire - Support), well-being (Cantril ladder and Satisfaction with Life Scale), ill-being (Beck Depression Inventory-II), emotional and behavioural problems (Adult Behavior Checklist), and life events (Bangor Life Events Schedule for Intellectual Disabilities). Results: Preliminary data analysis shows significant relationships between need satisfaction, autonomous motivation, and well-being, and between need frustration and ill-being. In addition, data are analysed to determine the strength of the prospective relationship. Implications: The results may give a much-needed boost to research and clinical practice on the psychological needs and motivational processes in people with ID.

Title: Self-harm and suicidal attempts - Are we aware enough?
Abstract Note: Introduction: Mental disorders are prevalent among individuals with certain disabilities. However, there is a lack of research on potential deleterious consequences such as self-harm or suicide attempts. This study investigated prevalence of psychiatric disorders and self-harm among four groups: Down syndrome (DS; n = 1298), intellectual disabilities (ID; n = 10671), autism spectrum disorder (ASD; n = 18625) and ADHD (n = 50353) compared to the rest of the population (2.3 million inhabitants) in the capital region of Sweden. Methods: We used administrative data for all healthcare including primary healthcare consultations with at least one recorded diagnosis of psychiatric disorders, self-harm, intentional or of undetermined intent used as a proxy for potential despair, pain or suicide attempt. Results: Psychiatric disorders as well as self-harm were less or equally prevalent among people with DS compared to the population in general. The prevalence were increased among individuals with ID, ASD and ADHD with OR between 1.53 and 9.01 for psychiatric disorders and between 4.42 and 16.67 for intentional self-harm compared to the population at large. Neighborhood socio-economic status affected the prevalence with a lower prevalence in wealthier areas. Implications: High prevalence of psychiatric disorders, self-harm and potential suicide attempts need to be investigated further with the target of improving care.

Title: Mental health and people with intellectual disabilities in england: What does secondary analysis of national cohort surveys tell us?
Abstract Note: Introduction: Secondary analysis of nationally representative cohort surveys, where a group of people with intellectual disabilities can be identified, can provide a useful perspective on the social determinants of mental health problems amongst people with intellectual disabilities. Methods: As part of the work of the Public Health England Learning Disabilities Observatory, a series of secondary analyses of nationally representative cohort surveys in England and the UK has been conducted, including surveys of children, young people, and adults. These include both proxy-reported and self-report measures of mental health and psychological distress. Results: These analyses fairly consistently report higher rates of mental health problems amongst people with intellectual disabilities compared to people without intellectual disabilities. These differences are typically partially accounted for by co-occurring differences in the social determinants of poor mental health, with discrimination and bullying as well as socio-economic factors robustly associated with poorer mental health. Implications: The importance of social determinants of mental health for people with intellectual disabilities from an early age is highlighted by these analyses. Limitations of such secondary analyses, particularly in terms of people with intellectual disabilities likely to be excluded from them, will also be discussed.

Title: Investigating the potential clinical utility of therapeutic techniques based on eidetic imagery (EI) as adapted by the eidetic model of growth (EMG) for people with intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Eidetic imagery (EI) is defined as a normal subjective predominantly visual image, which may or may not to be related to experiences of an actual situation. It is accompanied by certain physiological and cognitive impact (Ahsen, 2010). The objective of this study was to investigate the clinical utility of therapeutic techniques based on EI (Ahsen, 1993; Syed, 2012) to address emotional, experiential and mental health issues in people with ID. Methods: Eidetic psychotherapy as adapted by Eidetic Model of Growth (Syed, 2012) was offered to 30 adults with ID in individual sessions. Participants were identified on the basis of their emotional, experiential, psychiatric and behavioural problems by their caregivers and recruited for the study after seeking consent. The Anxiety, Depression and Mood Scale (ADAMS) was administered before therapy, after every 5th session and after the termination of therapy. Results: The analysis revealed a significant difference in the pretherapy and post-therapy scores on the ADAMS (with large effect size d = 1,54) and on its all subscales. Implications: The results indicate a promising utility of therapeutic techniques based on eidetic imagery for people with ID. For generalization and replicability of results, a randomised controlled trial is needed with more objective definition of inclusion/exclusion criteria.

Title: Psychological adjustment of siblings of people with an autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability or another developmental disabilitiy: Scoping review
Abstract Note: Introduction: Problematic behaviors, such as physical aggression on others or on themselves, are reported in approximately 60%of people with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), Intellectual Disability (ID) or another developmental delay (DD). Their siblings growing up in the same environment are thus confronted to these behaviors and several studies point out the possibility of greater anxiety symptoms for those siblings than for the siblings of typically developing child. Methods: A scoping review was carried out to figure out the state of knowledge on the psychological adjustment of brothers and sisters of children or adults with an ASD, an ID or a DD when they present problematic behaviors. The methodology by Arksey et O'Malley was used for this scoping review. Results: 474 articles were found with the research strategy and 93 of those were retained as relevant and read entirely. The purpose of this presentation is to describe the methodology and the results of this scoping review. Implications: The ultimate objective is to elaborate a specific question for a future research to better understand the psychological mechanisms that they implement in order to adapt to this reality and thereby suggest interventions for them and their family in order to enhance their quality of life.

Title: Understanding the relationship between child behaviour and parental well-being: The role of parental self-efficacy, social support and financial hardship as moderators
Abstract Note: Introduction: Child behaviour problems are established predictors of parental well-being in families of children with intellectual disabilities (ID). Few studies have explored factors that may moderate the relationship between child behaviour and well-being in parents of young children with ID. Methods: Parents of young children (18 months to 5 years) with ID were recruited for a cluster-randomised feasibility study investigating a group-based parenting programme across three sites in the UK. Baseline data included measures of child behaviour and emotional problems, parental well-being, parenting efficacy, and social support. Results: Baseline data was collected for 74 primary caregivers across three sites. Two-level linear regression models will be used to explore the association between child behaviour problems and parental well-being, and the extent to which this will be moderated by other variables (e.g., parenting efficacy, social support, financial hardship). Final results will be presented at the Congress. Implications: Developing an understanding of potential moderators may provide support for the need for early intervention (e.g., social support, parenting efficacy), and inform future early intervention development and targeted provision for parents of young children with ID.

Title: Social schemas linkages with social information processing: Similarities found for youth with mild intellectual disability, borderline IQ, and average IQ
Abstract Note: Introduction: Negative social schemas (SS) about the world and the self are found to link with social information processing (SIP) of new situations. If and how SS and SIP associate for youth with mild intellectual disability (MID: IQ50-70), borderline intelligence (BIQ: 71- 84), and average intelligence (AIQ ≥ 85) is however unclear. Similarities and differences in these linkages were examined for youth with MID compared to peers. Methods: 232 13-to-17-year-olds participated (M = 15.2 SD = 1.33, 54% male). Wechsler's scales of intelligence measured IQ (Wechsler, 1949; 1955). SS were assessed with the Youth Personality Inventory- Mistrust scale (Luteijn et al., 2005), Childhood Narcissism-scale (Thomaes et al., 2008), and Sensitivity to Disrespect-scale (MacDonald, 2008). Videos with social problem situations assessed SIP-steps: intent attribution, response-generation, self-efficacy for aggression. Results: For all youth, higher mistrust related to higher self-efficacy for aggression. Sensitivity to disrespect linked with higher hostile intent attribution. Narcissism characteristics associated with higher hostile intent attribution and self-efficacy for aggression. Relations between SS and SIP were found above and beyond influences of IQ on SIP and were similar across IQ-groups. Implications: These results provide insight in similar cognitive processes from SS to SIP in youth with MID compared with their peers. Future cognitive-behavioural treatments may include this knowledge on similar cognitive processes instead of focusing on differences when treating youth with MID.

Title: Lessons about learning disability: Encouraging positive perceptions of people with intellectual disabilities in scottish schools
Abstract Note: Introduction: Pupils with intellectual disabilities are one of the most bullied groups in the school system and in local communities. Moreover, young people also play a significant role in hate crimes against people with intellectual disabilities of all ages beyond the school gates. This paper describes the development of a research informed programme of lessons for children in mainstream secondary schools, aimed at counteracting bullying towards people with intellectual disabilities by promoting empathy and more positive attitudes towards them. Methods: A literature review, a review of current practice and the experiences and views of young people with intellectual disabilities and their families all contributed to the development of the programme. Data from subsequent piloting and feasibility work was used to finalise the programme. Results: The final five lessons concern: i) difference and disability, ii) an understanding of intellectual disability, iii) the nature and impact of disablist bullying towards people with intellectual disabilities and iv) opportunities for inclusion. Implications: One implication of this work is that that there needs to be further research to explore the impact of school based interventions, promoting an understanding of people with intellectual disabilities, in the wider community. Teachers delivering the lessons may have greater influence than transitory campaigns to counteract bullying and promote positive attitudes towards people with intellectual disabilities.

Title: Measuring the fidelity of interventions among people with intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Steps to Effective Problem-Solving program (STEPS) is an NIH funded efficacy clinical trial. Hypothesized results are improved social problem-solving skills and reduced problem behaviors in group homes receiving STEPS versus our attention-control Food for Life. One outcome of clinical trials is moving interventions into widescale dissemination; for this, it is important to evaluate implementation fidelity, which includes evaluating social and communication competence in facilitation of interventions. As part of the clinical trial, the purpose of this work was to develop scoring examples for Breitenstein's Fidelity Checklist, in order to ensure reliability in evaluating and scoring the fidelity our interventions. The Aims were to: 1) identify examples of specific competence skills, such as appropriately reinforcing participants' ideas and facilitating sharing of ideas in the STEPS and Food for Life interventions; and 2) provide examples that differentiate scores 1-3 on competence skills. Methods: Two coders independently checked audiotaped sessions from seven group homes in both conditions, seven from STEPS and seven Food for Life and together developed adherence coding examples. Results: We provide and discuss examples of statements and behaviors for each competence item score added to Breitenstein's coding manual. Implications: This work improves our knowledge of evaluating intervention implementation fidelity among people with ID.

Title: 'Pudelwohl'- part 2: A mental well-being app for people with intellectual disabilities and their support worker: Pilot data
Abstract Note: Introduction: Digital mental health interventions for people with intellectual disabilities are scarce, despite the abundance of such mainstream interventions. We aimed to develop and evaluate the feasibility of a four-week tablet application to improve the mental wellbeing of people with intellectual disabilities. Methods: Using a within-subjects pre-posttest design, twelve men with mild to moderate intellectual disabilities (median age = 19 years) and their support workers (median age = 42 years) completed four weekly sessions, lasting approximately 30-40 minutes each. Preliminary effectiveness was assessed using self-reported well-being (Personal Wellbeing Index - Intellectual Disability; PWI-ID) and with the support worker completed Aberrant Behaviour Checklist - Community (ABCC). Participants with ID also completed mood barometers prior to every session. Results: Mood ratings increased for five and decreased for two participants. No changes were observed in PWI-ID ratings, whilst proxyratings of behavioural problems decreased (Wilcoxon signed rank test, Z = -1.967, p = .049). Implications: The findings are inconclusive, yet suggest that a digital well-being intervention for joint use by people with intellectual disabilities and their support workers might have some benefits. Differences in outcome measures indicate these are sensitive to detecting potential intervention benefits. Piloting the intervention in a (sub-)clinical sample would be a next step.

Title: Satisfaction and frustration of basic psychological needs in highly (socially) anxious adolescents with mild intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Frustration of Basic Psychological Needs (BPN) is related to ill-being, like anxiety, while satisfaction of BPN is linked to well-being. These associations have also been explored among adolescents and also among adults with mild intellectual disabilities (MID). On this basis, the hypothesis was tested that satisfaction of BPN is lower and frustration of BPN is higher in anxious adolescents than in non-anxious adolescents with MID. Methods: Data were collected on anxiety and basic psychological needs (N = 230; age range 12-19 years; 47.4% male). To measure anxiety, we used the SCARED; to measure BPN we used the BPNSFSID. Data were collected in schools for adolescents with MID and in a residential treatment setting for adolescents with MID and behavioural problems. Results: Preliminary results indicate that scores on frustration of all three Basic Psychological Needs is strongly and positively correlated with the SCARED (for all factors the correlation was significant at 0.01 level). Correlations between BPN satisfaction and SCARED failed to reach conventional levels of significance. Implications: Implications of the findings will be discussed for the conceptualization of associated factors in current models for understanding and treating anxiety in adolescents with MID.

Title: Which student problem behaviors are sources of teacher stress in special needs schools?
Abstract Note: Introduction: Students with intellectual disabilities (ID) in special needs schools often exhibit high levels of problem behaviors (Dekker & Koot, 2003). Besides of the challenges for students and their parents, behavioural problems can also be a source of stress for teachers (Hastings & Brown, 2002). However, less is known on which behaviors are perceived as how stressful in special needs schools. Methods: Using paper-pencil questionnaires, 233 special needs teachers (M = 48.1 years (SD = 10.1); 83.7% female) in Switzerland provided information on how stressful (0 = not stressful to 3 = very stressful) they perceived different types of students' behavioural problems. The 93 behavior descriptions stemmed from the Developmental Behavior Checklist (Einfeld & Tonge, 2002) and the scale demonstrated excellent reliability (α = .98). Results: Preliminary results from the ongoing data collection suggest that “Hits or kicks others” (M = 1.79, SD = .99), “Bites others” (M = 1.57, SD = 1.20) and “Runs away with intention” (M = 1.57, SD = 1.04) were reported as the greatest sources of stress. Results presented will include further analyses using the final data set. Implications: Implications for special needs teachers' well-being will be discussed with a specific focus on the role of students' externalizing behaviors.

Title: A review of the roles and practice domains of Australian nurses who work with people with intellectual and developmental disability
Abstract Note: Introduction: Nurses who work with people with intellectual and developmental disability (IDD) provide specific and vital health-related care. This study reports Australian survey data about the roles and practice domains of these nurses, as a first step in reconceptualising the future roles of Australian nurses. Methods: An anonymous online survey was used to collect data about the roles of nurses across physical, behavioural, mental health, and adaptive behaviour domains. Results: Approximately 144 survey responses were captured, of which 95 had completed data (74 female, 19 male). The most common forms of physical care included gastrointestinal (88.6%), neurological/sensory (86%), musculoskeletal (81%), and respiratory (81%). Sexual health care was notably lower (39%). Support for self-harming behaviour was the most frequently endorsed behavioural care (84%), followed by behaviours that are harmful to others (79%) and unusual or repetitive behaviours (76%). Communicating needs was endorsed by 94% of the nurses for adaptive behaviour. For mental health, nurses were most likely to support symptoms of anxiety (77%), followed by depression (69%) and serious self-harm (62%). Implications: Although nurses provide high levels of physical healthcare, their roles also extend to support for sexual health, behavioural, and adaptive behaviour. Diversity of nursing skills is critical when caring for people with IDD and this has implications for the future reconceptualization of the nursing role.

Title: Housing design strategies and adaptations for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities and complex behavioural needs: A scoping review
Abstract Note: Introduction: Environmental/architectural characteristics of housing are fundamental to supportive living for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) and complex behavioural needs. Adaptations to the physical environment are one strategy to reduce aggressive or self-injurious behaviours. However, there remains limited understanding about the physical characteristics of successful housing for this population. The aim of this literature review is to summarise existing research on housing designed for individuals with IDD and complex behavioural needs. Methods: We searched electronic databases and examined reference lists of relevant publications for peer reviewed qualitative and quantitative studies. No year or age restriction was applied. Two reviewers applied inclusion criteria to identified studies. Study characteristics and results were summarized in tables. Results: Thematic analysis of 15 papers identified that durability, safety, stimulation and homelikeness were parameters that influence quality of life and the likelihood of a successful residential placement. Despite the identification of several contributing factors, research to date fails to clearly define strategies to physically adapt residences for individuals with IDD that address complex behavioural needs specifically. Implications: This review presents gaps in the literature of an important area that could have policy implications for effective supported living and cost implications by avoiding construction or renovation of unsuitable housing. The results of this review support current, ongoing research on successful housing for adults with IDD.

Title: Effects of sport and physical activity on behaviour and emotional problems and psychosocial outcomes in children and adolescents with intellectual disability: A systematic review
Abstract Note: Introduction: While there is increasing information available about the physical benefits of sport and physical activity, there is a lack of research into the potential benefits it may have for behaviour and emotional problems and psychosocial outcomes in children with intellectual disability. This review aimed to collate the available research in this area. Methods: Five databases (Ovid MedLine, PsycINFO, ERIC, SportDISCUS & SCOPUS) were systematically searched using terms relating to sport and physical activity, behaviour and emotional problems, psychosocial outcomes, intellectual disability, and children and adolescents. Articles were excluded if not written in English. Results: The initial search found 2409 references in the five databases. After duplicates were removed, 1718 references were screened on title and abstract. 189 articles were included in the full text review, from which 29 were identified as eligible. A variety of physical activities were examined with different outcome measures, with the majority indicating positive outcomes from participation in any level of sport and physical activity. Implications: Studies examining outcomes from participation in physical activity for children with ID varied greatly in terms of scope and design. Results of the review indicated a need for more rigorous and detailed studies, especially clinical trials, with larger sample sizes and a wider range of covariates in order to determine the potential benefits to children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities.

Title: Exploring the effects using T-jackets on the behaviours of adults with autism spectrum disorders (ASD)
Abstract Note: Introduction: T-jacket is a remotely-controlled variable air pressure vest that provides deep touch pressure on the body's joints and muscles via a mobile app, to calm individuals facing sensory modulation difficulties, stress and anxiety. This study aims to determine whether T-jackets would improve the on-seat, on-task and self-stimulatory behaviours of adults with ASD. Methods: 25 participants aged above 18 were recruited from Day Activity Centres. They were randomly assigned into 2 groups. The Adult Sensory Profile, Behaviour Problem Inventory for individual with Intellectual Disabilities -Short Form (BPI-S), videos and observation charts were used to measure on-seat, on-task, and selfstimulatory behaviours. 18 intervention sessions were conducted and each session comprised of a 15 minute table top activity for both groups, with one group being administered with T-jackets. After a 2 weeks cooling-off period, there was crossover of intervention for another 18 sessions. Results: Preliminary results revealed that participants who wore Tjackets showed improvements in on-seat, on task and reduce selfstimulatory behaviours during the table top activities. The study is ongoing and the findings will be presented at the conference. Implications: The results of the study supports the utility of the Tjacket to improve the participation levels and quality of life of adults with ASD.

Title: Housing design strategies and adaptations for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities and complex behavioural needs: Key informant interviews
Abstract Note: Introduction: In Ontario, Canada, adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) struggle to find living arrangements that appropriately meet their behavioural needs, including aggression and selfinjury. Although there is no single underlying cause for this behaviour, it is important to remember that such behaviour is often a response to the environment, particularly when there is poor support or physical space adaptations. Despite this, few studies describe support models and physical environment adaptations for people with IDD who exhibit complex behavioural needs. Methods: This study conducted 19 interviews. Interviewees included persons with IDD living in high support homes, high support home developmental and maintenance staff, and health professionals. A semistructured interview guide with questions related to space adaptations and residential models was used. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and were independently coded by two researchers, who came to consensus on themes and sub-themes. Results: The most common themes related to environmental adaptations, client safety, and staff safety. Specifically, participants described successful environmental adaptations including creating environments with separate living spaces for residents, and more open spaces with less furniture and better sight lines. Implications: Results of this study intend to inform funding and planning of successful residential placements for persons with IDD, including space and design recommendations.

Title: Psychological and body-related consequences in individuals with intellectual disability with a history of sexual abuse. an overview of the literature
Abstract Note: Introduction: Sexual abuse in individuals with normal IQ results in a wide range of psychological and body-related consequences. Whether consequences of sexual abuse are similar for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID) is as yet unknown. The aim of the review is to provide an overview of the psychological and body-related consequences of sexually abused in individuals with ID. Methods: Databases were searched for publication between the years 1998 and 2018. Two independent reviewers assessed studies for inclusion, which resulted in seven studies. Results: Psychological consequences could be divided into five themes: challenging behaviour, sexualized behaviour, and three psychiatric disorders, namely anxiety, depression and posttraumatic stress. Two body-related consequences were found: low body-esteem and poor feelings of personal safety. Some psychological consequences, such as aggression and hyperarousal, might also be regarded as related to the body. Implications: Sexual abuse in individuals with ID results in psychological as well as body-related consequences. However, no general conclusion could be drawn because none of the included studies were experimental or longitudinal. Furthermore, no standardised diagnostic instruments were used that specifically assesses the consequences of sexual abuse in individuals with ID. Future research is needed to develop and validate psychological and bodyrelated diagnostic instruments for this group. The interrelationship of psychological and body-related consequence also deserve to be studied in future research.

Title: Assessing anger related interoceptive awareness in individuals with mild intellectual disabilities and borderline intellectual functioning
Abstract Note: Introduction: Individuals with MID-BIF are often referred for treatment due to aggressive behaviour. Psychomotor therapy (PMT), a body-oriented approach, has shown to be a promising treatment for individuals with MID-BIF exhibiting aggression. One PMT-aim is raising interoceptive awareness (IA), in order to recognise anger, as it is a precursor for aggression. To evaluate PMT in this population, a specific instrument is needed. Therefor the psychometric characteristics of the Anger Bodily Sensations Questionnaire for individuals with MID-BIF (ABSQ for MID-BIF) are tested. Methods: Test-retest reliability and internal consistency were examined in 172 individuals. Construct validity was measured by correlations with the scores of the ZAV [Zelf-analyse vragenlijst - boosheidsdispositie], the Dutch adaption on of State Trait Anger Scale (subscale anger state) and Social and Dysfunction Scale (SDAS). Results: Cronbach's α = .87, mean inter item correlation is.27 (SD = 0.10) with a range between.004 and.59. ICC ranges between.61 and.79, all correlations are statistically significant with p < .01. Mean proportion of exact and adjacent agreement are.51 and.81, respectively. Spearman correlation is.53 with a range between.44 and.64. Significant correlations are found for both ZAV (anger disposition) and SDAS. Implications: ABSQ for MID-BIF has an adequate test-retest reliability and a good internal consistency. This instrument can be used in clinical practice for both diagnostic and treatment evaluation purposes.

Title: Dietary supplements to reduce challenging behavior among people with intellectual disabilities: A qualitative study
Abstract Note: Introduction: In the literature there is some evidence for the use of dietary supplements to reduce aggression and other rule offending behavior. In the field of intellectual disability care this intervention has never been studied. The degree of acceptance of the intervention by clients, their representatives and professionals influences the success of a future implementation. Therefore, it is important to detect potential barriers against, and opportunities for, implementation. The study aimed to reveal these factors through focus group interviews among clients and professionals. Methods: At least four focus group sessions were conducted; two exclusively for people with intellectual disability. Client focus groups consisted of a maximum of six participants. The other focus groups, consisting of professionals and client represents had a maximum of ten participants. The focus group audio materials were transcribed and analysed using dedicated software, following the steps of 'constant comparison analysis'. Results: Preliminary results are categorised into a main theme and several subthemes. Implications: Our results determine implementation strategies of a putative intervention with dietary supplements of people with intellectual disabilities.

Title: EEG Abnormalities as a Neurophysiological Biomarker of Severity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Pilot Cohort Study
Abstract Note: To date, the phenotypic significance of EEG abnormalities in patients with ASD is unclear. In a population affected by ASD we aimed to evaluate: the phenotypic characteristics; the prevalence of EEG abnormalities; the potential correlations between EEG abnormalities and behavioral and cognitive variables. Sixty-nine patients with ASD underwent cognitive or developmental testing, language assessment, and adaptive behavior skills evaluation as well as sleep/wake EEG recording. EEG abnormalities were found in 39.13% of patients. EEG abnormalities correlated with autism severity, hyperactivity, anger outbursts, aggression, negative or destructive behavior, motor stereotypies, intellectual disability, language impairment and self-harm. Our findings confirmed that EEG abnormalities are present in the ASD population and correlate with several associated phenotypic features.

Title: Stigma experienced by families of individuals with intellectual disabilities and autism: A systematic review
Abstract Note: Studies have investigated the experiences of courtesy stigma and affiliate stigma in family members of individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) without a clear distinction between the two. This systematic literature review aimed to evaluate the findings of studies that examined the experiences of stigma in families of individuals with intellectual disabilities and/or autism. A systematic search of PsycINFO, ERIC and Scopus identified relevant articles published between 2012 and 2016, to expand on an earlier review on this topic published in 2012. Ten articles pertaining to eight studies were identified. They revealed that family carers do experience stigma and various consequences related to these, with family culture influencing these experiences. This review identifies a number of psychosocial variables that are associated with the development of courtesy stigma, affiliate stigma and their consequences. It highlights protective factors and strategies family carers use to cope with stigma, and a lack of clarity in distinguishing the concepts of courtesy stigma and affiliate stigma in family members.

Title: Adults with Down syndrome: a comprehensive approach to manage complexity
Abstract Note: Background: Down syndrome (DS) is characterised by premature ageing that affects selected organ systems, and persons with this condition can present patterns of co-morbidities and deficits often observed in the older population without DS. However, information on the characteristics of adult persons with DS is limited. The objective of the study is to describe characteristics of adults with DS collected with a standardised, comprehensive assessment instrument. Methods: Cross-sectional study. Four hundred thirty adults with DS (age range 18/75 years) from three countries (Italy, n = 95; USA, n = 175; and Canada, n = 160). A standardised assessment instrument (interRAI intellectual disability) was used to assess sample characteristics. Results: Mean age ranged from 35.2 (standard deviation 12.0) years in the US sample to 48.8 (standard deviation 9.0) years in the Canadian sample. Most participants in the Italian and US sample were living in private homes, while more than half of those in the Canadian sample were institutionalised. Prevalences of geriatric conditions, including cognitive deficits, disability in the common activities of daily living, symptoms of withdrawal or anhedonia, aggressive behaviour, communication problems, falls and hearing problems were high in the study sample. Gastrointestinal symptoms, skin and dental problems and obesity were also frequently observed. Conclusions: Adults with DS present with a high level of complexity, which may suggest the need for an approach based on a comprehensive assessment and management that can provide adequate care. Further research is needed to understand better the effectiveness of such an approach in the DS population.

Title: Factors associated with depression and anxiety in children with intellectual disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: Individuals with intellectual disabilities (ID) are at increased risk for depression and anxiety disorders; however, there is a paucity of research that pertains to associative factors for these mental health disorders in this population. The objective of this investigation was to determine factors associated with depression and anxiety problems in children with ID. Methods: Children 6–17 years with ID (n = 423; 63% male) from the 2016 National Survey of Children's Health were included in this cross-sectional study. Outcome measures included depression and anxiety problems. Predictor variables included sociodemographics, ID severity, co-morbid conditions (autism spectrum disorders, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, Down syndrome and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), physical factors (i.e. physical activity, sleep duration and pain) and social factors (e.g. participation in activities and bully victimisation). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to determine the association between all factors and depression and/or anxiety problems among children with ID. Results: The prevalence of depression and/or anxiety problems was 35.4%. After adjusting for sociodemographics, Hispanic race was associated with lower odds [odds ratio (OR), 0.3; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.1–0.8] of depression and/or anxiety problems. After adjusting for race, co-morbid conditions, and physical and social factors, autism spectrum disorders (OR, 4.4; 95% CI, 1.1–10.1), Down syndrome (OR, 0.2; 95% CI, 0.1–0.8), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (OR, 5.9; 95% CI, 2.5–14.3), pain (OR, 7.0; 95% CI, 2.9–17.1) and bully victimisation (OR 2.3; 95% CI, 1.0–5.3) were each associated with depression and/or anxiety problems. Conclusions: The present study identified both treatable and modifiable, as well as unmodifiable, factors associated with depression and/or anxiety problems in children with ID.

Title: Behaviour problems in people with intellectual disabilities: validation of the French version of the Behaviour Problems Inventory – Short Form
Abstract Note: Objective: The risk for the development of severe behaviour problems by individuals with intellectual disability (ID) is a well-known concern. However, there are currently no reliable instruments for assessing these behaviours in French. The Behaviour Problems Inventory – Short Form (BPI-S) assesses these three types of behaviour in people with ID: self-injurious behaviour (eight items), aggressive/destructive behaviours (10 items) and stereotypic behaviours (12 items). The purpose of this study was to conduct a psychometric study of a French version of the BPI-S. Method: Data were collected on 305 children, adolescents and young adults with ID 50 care workers in seven specialised institutions in France as informants. We examined the scale's factorial structure (using confirmatory factor analysis), internal consistency and inter-rater reliability. We also established preliminary French norms. Results: Our results show that the French BPI-S has a factorial structure similar to that of the English version. It has good internal consistency. The internal consistency of the frequency ratings was 0.91 and 0.62 for the severity ratings. The BPI-S has a good inter-rater reliability with acceptable coefficients for the frequency ratings (Self Injurious Behaviour (SIB) = 0.81; Aggressive–Destructive behaviour = 0.66; Stereotyped behaviours = 0.75) and for the severity ratings (SIB = 0.92; Aggressive–Destructive behaviour = 0.54). The data also show that the frequency and severity of behaviours differ based on the level of ID. Conclusions: The French version of the BPI-S has good psychometric properties for assessing problem behaviours in children, adolescents and young adults. This scale can be used for research and clinical evaluation of disorders associated with ID.

Title: Mental health and behavioural problems in children with XXYY: a comparison with intellectual disabilities
Abstract Note: Background: The phenotype of children with XXYY has predominantly been defined by comparison to other sex chromosome aneuploidies trisomies affecting male children; however, the intellectual ability of children with XXYY is lower than children with other sex chromosome aneuploidies trisomies. It is not known to what extent the phenotype identified to date is specific to XXYY, rather than a reflection of lower IQ. This study evaluates the mental health and behaviour of children with XXYY, in comparison to children with intellectual disabilities of heterogeneous genetic origin. Methods: Fifteen children with XXYY and 30 controls matched for age (4–14 years), sex and intellectual ability were ascertained from the IMAGINE ID study. IMAGINE ID participants have intellectual disabilities due to genetic anomalies confirmed by National Health Service Regional Genetic Centre laboratories. The mental health and behaviour of participants was examined with the Development and Well-being Assessment and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. Results: Children with XXYY experienced significantly more frequent and intense temper outbursts than the control group. Conclusion: Our results suggest that temper outbursts may be specifically associated with the XXYY phenotype. These problems have a significant impact on the daily lives of boys with XXYY and their families. It is crucial to ensure that families are well supported to manage these difficulties.

Title: A 'choice', an 'addiction', a way 'out of the lost': Exploring self-injury in autistic people without intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Background: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) describes a phenomenon where individuals inflict deliberate pain and tissue damage to their bodies. Self-injurious behaviour is especially prevalent across the autism spectrum, but little is understood about the features and functions of self-injury for autistic individuals without intellectual disability, or about the risk factors that might be valuable for clinical usage in this group. Methods: One hundred and three autistic adults who responded to an online advertisement were classified as current, historic or non-self-harmers in accordance with responses to the Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Assessment Tool (NSSI-AT). Multinomial regression aimed to predict categorisation of participants in accordance with scores on tests of autistic traits, alexithymia, depression, anxiety, mentalising and sensory sensitivity. Linear regression examined relationships between these predictors and the range, frequency, lifetime occurrence and functional purposes of NSSI. Qualitative analysis explored the therapeutic interventions that participants had found helpful, and what they wished people understood about self-injury. Results: Current, historic and non-self-harming participants did not differ in age, age at diagnosis, male-to-female ratio, level of employment or education (the majority qualified to at least degree level). The most common function of NSSI was the regulation of low-energy affective states (depression, dissociation), followed by the regulation of high-energy states such as anger and anxiety. Alexithymia significantly predicted the categorisation of participants as current, historic or non-self-harmers, and predicted use of NSSI for regulating high-energy states and communicating distress to others. Depression, anxiety and sensory-sensitivity also differentiated participant groups, and sensory differences also predicted the range of bodily areas targeted, lifetime incidence and frequency of NSSI. Sensory differences, difficulty expressing and identifying emotions also emerged as problematic in the qualitative analysis, where participants expressed the need for compassion, patience, non-judgement and the need to recognise diversity between self-harmers, with some participants perceiving NSSI as a practical, non-problematic coping strategy. Conclusions: Alexithymia, depression, anxiety and sensory differences may place some autistic individuals at especial risk of self-injury. Investigating the involvement of these variables and their utility for identification and treatment is of high importance, and the voices of participants offer guidance to practitioners confronted with NSSI in their autistic clients.

Title: Metyrosine treatment in a woman with chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and psychosis: a case study
Abstract Note: Background: People with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DS) are assumed to be especially vulnerable to developing mental illness such as psychosis. Aim: The study was established to contribute to knowledge about metyrosine medication in patients with 22q11.2 DS and psychosis. Methods: A case study was established including a woman with intellectual disability, 22q11.2 DS, and psychosis. Metyrosine medication was implemented, as conventional anti-psychotic medication was unsuccessful. Results: Effect of metyrosine medication included both psychotic symptom relief with decreased aggressive behaviour. Adjunctive milieu therapy contributed to complience. Conclusion: For patients with 22q11.2 DS and psychosis, metyrosine medication may prove effective. However, there are significant ethical dilemmas related to metyrosine medication for psychotic symptoms.

Title: Inpatient Psychiatric Treatment of Serious Behavioral Problems in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD): Specialized Versus General Inpatient Units
Abstract Note: Psychiatric hospitalization of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is common, but there is little comparative information available on different psychiatric hospital treatment models. Children with ASD ages 4–20 were enrolled upon admission to either a specialized (N = 53) or a general child psychiatric unit (N = 27). Caregivers completed the Aberrant Behavioral Checklist-Irritability Sub-scale (ABC-I) at admission, discharge, and 2 months post-discharge and reported information on crisis service utilization 2 months post-discharge. Children treated in the specialized unit had lower ABC-I scores at discharge and 2 months post-discharge (F = 8.98, p = 0.003) and were significantly less likely to experience an ER visit within 2 months post-discharge (X2 = 5.51, p = 0.019). Specialized inpatient units may be more effective for children with ASD in need of psychiatric hospitalization.

Title: Intellectual, adaptive and behavioural characteristics in four patients with 18p deletion syndrome
Abstract Note: Background: The association of behavioural phenotype assessment with cytogenomic characterisation may provide a better comprehension of genotype–phenotype correlations in syndromes caused by chromosomal abnormalities, such as 18p deletion syndrome. Method: We report on four Brazilian patients with 18p deletion syndrome characterised by cytogenomic techniques and detailed neuropsychological evaluation. Intellectual, adaptive and behavioural characteristics were assessed through the Wechsler's Scales, the Vineland-II Scale and the Child Behaviour Checklist, respectively. Socio-economic measures including main caretaker educational level and family income as defined by Brazilian criteria for social class classification were also collected to evaluate a possible contribution of environmental factors in neurocognitive variability. Results: Two out of four patients showed intellectual disability (IQ < 70). Wechsler's scale results suggest that in our sample, interpretation of social situations based on observation of non-verbal behaviour constitute a cognitive strength while judgement of social rules and language skills associated with word knowledge and verbal fluency may be a cognitive weakness. Concerning adaptive behaviour, motor and socialisation domains showed to better develop than communication and daily living skills on the Vineland-II Scale. Only one patient presented internalising behavioural problems based on the Child Behaviour Checklist. Our results also suggested that socio-economic status may contribute to overall patient development. Conclusion: Our results suggest that some 18p deletion syndrome patients may present average intellectual performance and that the segment deletion size and some families' socio-economic conditions may influence cognitive development.

Title: Task Dependency When Evaluating Association Between Facial Emotion Recognition and Facial Emotion Expression in Children with ASD
Abstract Note: The impact of facial emotion recognition (FER) deficits on facial emotion expression (FEE) during interaction with a novel computerized system was investigated in children with ASD (n = 20), in comparison to typically developing (TD) peers (n = 20). Although there was not clear evidence of impaired FEE, children with ASD showed more atypical FEE. In children with ASD, better FER predicted better FEE when the participants were asked to express a labeled emotion (t(18) = − 2.75, p =.01, d = 1.24). The stronger relationship between FER and FEE in children with ASD, relative to controls, suggests that intervention targeting social communication deficits might have maximal effect when both processes are considered.

Title: Neurodevelopmental correlates of behavioural and emotional problems in a neuropaediatric sample
Abstract Note: Most research does not address the overlap between neurodevelopmental disorders when investigating concomitant mental health problems. The purpose of the present study was to examine the association of intellectual disability (ID), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) with the presence of behavioural and emotional problems after controlling for other well-known correlates and risk factors. The sample included 4- to 18-year-old children who attended neuropaediatric clinics (N = 331). After controlling for adversity, age, gender, other developmental/neurological disorders, parental emotional problems, and parenting strategies, the presence of ADHD but not ASD or ID was uniquely associated with behaviour problems. Neither ADHD nor ASD nor ID was significantly associated with emotional problems after controlling for other risk factors. However, ADHD, ASD and behavioural/emotional disorders but not ID were significantly associated with functional impairment in everyday activities after controlling for other risk factors. Because children with neurodevelopmental disorders have complex needs, a holistic approach to diagnosis and interventions is highly warranted, including the assessment and treatment of behavioural and emotional disorders.

Title: Friendships and social participation as markers of quality of life of adolescents and adults with fragile X syndrome and autism
Abstract Note: Friendships and social participation are key domains of quality of life for individuals with intellectual disabilities. This study examined the friendships, social and recreational activities, and family social networks of individuals with intellectual disabilities from two distinct diagnostic groups: individuals diagnosed with fragile X syndrome (n = 81) compared with those diagnosed with autistic disorder (n = 226). Within each diagnostic group, individuals in two developmental stages were compared: adolescence and adulthood. Quality of life in friendships and social participation domains was notably low for individuals with fragile X and those with autism. Individuals with fragile X had more friendships and a less negative social impact on the family than individuals with autism. Across both groups, adolescents spent less time with friends and neighbors, and more time in exercising, than did adults.

Title: Factors associated with DSM-5 severity level ratings for autism spectrum disorder
Abstract Note: The newest edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (5th ed., DSM-5) introduced substantial changes to the diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder, including new severity level ratings for social communication and restricted and repetitive behavior domains. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the use of these new severity ratings and to examine their relation to other measures of severity and clinical features. Participants included 248 children with autism spectrum disorder who received diagnostic evaluations at one of six Autism Treatment Network sites. Higher severity ratings in both domains were associated with younger age, lower intelligence quotient, and greater Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule–Second Edition domain-specific symptom severity. Greater restricted and repetitive behavior severity was associated with higher parent-reported stereotyped behaviors. Severity ratings were not associated with emotional or behavioral problems. The new DSM-5 severity ratings in both domains were significantly associated with behavioral observations of autism severity but not with measures of other behavioral or emotional symptoms. However, the strong associations between intelligence quotient and DSM-5 severity ratings in both domains suggest that clinicians may be including cognitive functioning in their overall determination of severity. Further research is needed to examine clinician decision-making and interpretation of these specifiers.

Title: Prevalence and sequelae of self-reported and other-reported sexual abuse in adults with intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Background: Sexual victimisation is an important problem that affects millions of people around the world, especially those with some kind of disability. The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of self-reported and documented sexual abuse in people with mild or moderate intellectual disability and to analyse the sequelae that such experiences can have on their psychosocial health. Methods: The sample consisted of 360 adults (50% men and 50% women) between 18 and 55 years of age (M = 39.87; standard deviation = 10.55). Results: The prevalence of sexual abuse is 6.10% when it is self-reported (9.4% in women and 2.8% in men) and 28.6% when it is reported by professionals (27.8% in women and 29.4% in men). People who self-report cases of abuse present poorer quality of life, more negative attitudes towards sex and a lower capacity to identify situations that entail a risk of sexual abuse. Individuals who have suffered documented cases of abuse are more likely to present encopresis, social isolation, self-harm and a higher number of suicide attempts. Conclusions: Our results evidence the need to have access to all sources of information so as to be able to obtain prevalence figures that match the real situation and to perform a proper analysis of the sequelae.

Title: Brief Report: Sibling Feelings Toward their Brother or Sister With or Without Autism or Intellectual Disability
Abstract Note: The present study examined 97 adolescent siblings of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD), or no disabilities. Siblings reported on their feelings toward their brother or sister (anxiety, hostility, and positive affect), and parents reported on general optimism, child behavior problems, and perceptions of how the child impacts the family, including the sibling. There were no differences between siblings of individuals with ASD and siblings of individuals with IDD on any sibling self-reported feelings toward their brother or sister, though parents of individuals with ASD reported significantly less optimism and more negative perception of the child’s impact on the family than did parents of children with IDD or no disability.

Title: Effects of social skills training using teaching strategies from applied behaviour analysis on the social skills of children with mild and moderate intellectual disabilities
Abstract Note: The present research aimed to study the effect of social skills training using the strategies from Applied Behavior Analysis on the social skills of children with mild and moderate intellectual disabilities at special schools of an Indian state. In a non-randomized pre-test post-test control group design, children with mild (n = 34) and moderate (n = 36) intellectual disabilities were placed into control and experimental group. Both the groups were tested with Social Skills Rating Scale devised by the researchers as a pre-test and as a post-test after intervention in social skills training to the experimental group. ANCOVA analysis indicated F (1, 31) =287.13, P=.00 for the children with mild intellectual disabilities, F (1, 33) =127.55, P=.00 for the children with moderate intellectual disabilities on Social Skill Rating Scale. Social skills training using teaching strategies from Applied Behaviour Analysis is an effective intervention for improving their social skills in all the domains of Social Skills Rating Scale. The program can be introduced at special schools in their daily curriculum to improve the social skills of the children with mild and moderate intellectual disabilities.

Title: Self-reported stress among adolescent siblings of individuals with autism spectrum disorder and Down syndrome
Abstract Note: Despite the prevalence of studies showing increased stress among mothers of individuals with autism spectrum disorders, few studies have examined general stress among typically developing siblings. This study used an online survey to compare the levels of self-reported stress between adolescent siblings of individuals with autism spectrum disorder and Down syndrome. Sibling of individuals with autism reported significantly more overall stress than did siblings of individuals with Down syndrome, as well as more stress specifically attributed to the brother/sister with autism. The two groups did not differ on perceived social support from family and friends. In linear regression models, the disability group (autism vs Down syndrome) was significantly related to sibling stress above and beyond target child behavior problems, perceived social support, and demographic factors. These results help shed light on the daily experiences of adolescent siblings of individuals with autism and call for more research into potential interventions to address increased stress levels.

Title: Talking about learning disability: promoting positive perceptions of people with intellectual disabilities in Scottish schools
Abstract Note: Pupils with intellectual disabilities are one of the most bullied groups in the school system and in local communities. Moreover, young people also play a significant role in hate crimes against people with intellectual disabilities of all ages beyond the school gates. This paper describes the development of a research informed program of lessons for children in mainstream secondary schools, aimed at counteracting bullying towards people with intellectual disabilities by promoting empathy and more positive attitudes towards them. A literature review, a review of current practice, and the experiences and views of young people with intellectual disabilities and their families all contributed to the development of the program. Data from subsequent piloting and feasibility work were used to finalize the program which consists of the following five lessons concerning: (i) difference and disability, (ii) an understanding of intellectual disability, (iii) the nature and impact of disablist bullying towards people with intellectual disabilities, and (iv) opportunities for inclusion. One conclusion from this work is that that there needs to be further research to explore the impact of school-based interventions, promoting an understanding of people with intellectual disabilities, in the wider community. Teachers delivering the lessons may have greater influence than transitory campaigns to counteract bullying and promote positive attitudes towards people with intellectual disabilities. However, a first step is to ensure that teachers delivering the lessons have an understanding of people with intellectual disabilities.

Title: Behavioral problems in children with autism spectrum disorder with and without co-occurring intellectual disability
Abstract Note: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), intellectual disability (ID), and behavioral problems commonly co-occur, leading to increased impairment, diagnostic confusion, and treatment delays. Using data from a large surveillance population of children with ASD, the objectives of the present study were to compare the relative risk of common behavioral problems in children with ASD, with and without co-occurring intellectual disability. Methods: Data from the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network (2006–2010) on 9378 8-year-old children who met case definition for ASD and had cognitive test scores and information on behavioral problems were analyzed using frequency measures, risk ratios, chi-squared tests, and trend tests. Results: Children with ASD with and without ID had on average six co-occurring behavioral problems. The relative risk (RR) of self-injurious behaviors, unusual fear responses, and eating abnormalities increased with increasing cognitive impairment among children with ASD and ID (all p<0.001). Conversely, RR of mood (p<0.001) and sleep abnormalities (p=0.013) declined with increasing levels of cognitive impairment. Conclusions: Children with ASD and ID are at greater risk of some behavioral problems and lower risk of others as compared to children with ASD only. Successful interventions depend on understanding the complex interactions between co-occurring neurodevelopmental and behavioral problems.

Title: Coaching parents to assess and treat self-injurious behaviour via telehealth
Abstract Note: The application of telehealth technology to conduct functional analysis (FA) and functional communication training (FCT) is emerging for children with developmental disabilities and behaviour support needs. The current study was designed to extend FA + FCT for self-injurious behaviour by using telehealth in home with parents as interventionists receiving real-time remote coaching. Two families with school-aged boys with developmental disabilities associated with intellectual disability participated, one with cerebral palsy and the other with autism spectrum disorder. Results indicated that parent-implemented FA + FCT via telehealth was effective for reducing self-injurious behaviour and increasing mands (communication requests) for both children. Both families successfully implemented the FA + FCT protocol with 95% overall fidelity via telehealth-supported coaching. Results are discussed in terms of their relationship to previous research, limitations and future directions.

Title: Persistence of self-injury, aggression and property destruction in children and adults with tuberous sclerosis complex
Abstract Note: Background: Individuals with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) are at increased risk of developing self-injurious behaviour. The persistence of this deleterious behaviour over years is reported in aetiologically heterogeneous samples to be between 60% and 80% but is unknown for TSC. Method: In this study, we determined the 3-year persistence of self-injury in a sample (n = 52) of children (with and without ID) and adults (with ID) with TSC and examined characteristics associated with persistence. Results: Findings for self-injury were contrasted to those for aggression and property destruction to examine the specificity of results to this behaviour. Self-injury was persistent in 84.6% of those with TSC who showed this behaviour, in contrast to 66.7% both for aggression and destruction. Persistent self-injury was associated with poor self-help skills, greater overactivity/impulsivity and more behavioural indicators of pain. These latter two characteristics were also associated with persistent aggression. No characteristics were associated with persistence of property destruction. Conclusion: These findings suggest that self-injurious behaviours in individuals with TSC, together with aggressive and destructive behaviours, are highly persistent and would benefit from targeted intervention. Poor adaptive skills, overactivity/impulsivity and painful health conditions may differentiate those at most risk for persistent self-injury or aggression.
